name: Eastern North Carolina barbecue
aliases: Eastern-style|Down East barbecue|whole-hog barbecue|Eastern Carolina barbecue
what: The whole pig, split and cooked over coals or on a gas or electric cooker, then chopped — skin, ham, shoulder, loin and belly together, 'every part of the hog except the squeal' — and dressed after cooking with a thin sauce of vinegar, salt, black pepper and crushed red pepper. No tomato. It is served with mayonnaise slaw, cornbread or hushpuppies, and often boiled potatoes, on a tray or a sandwich with the slaw on the meat. The style belongs to the Coastal Plain east of Raleigh; Ayden, Goldsboro, Wilson, Kinston, Rocky Mount and Greenville are its towns.

name: Lexington-style barbecue
aliases: Lexington barbecue|Piedmont-style barbecue|Western-style barbecue|Western North Carolina barbecue
what: Pork shoulders cooked slowly over hardwood coals, usually hickory, then chopped, coarse-chopped or sliced and dressed with a thin red sauce the Piedmont calls dip: vinegar, ketchup or tomato, water, salt, pepper and red pepper, sweeter or hotter by the house. It comes with red slaw — cabbage dressed with the same dip instead of mayonnaise — and hushpuppies, on a tray or a bun. The style belongs to the Piedmont west of Raleigh. Lexington, a Davidson County town of about 20,000 that calls itself the Barbecue Capital of the World and counted more than twenty barbecue restaurants in 2003, is its center; Greensboro, Salisbury, Shelby and High Point are its other towns.

name: Heavy tomato barbecue
aliases: heavy-tomato style|tomato-and-sugar barbecue|Upstate barbecue|western South Carolina barbecue
what: Pork shoulders and butts, ribs and chicken cooked over hickory or on cookers and served with a thick, sweet, red sauce of tomato, brown sugar or molasses, vinegar and spices — the sauce the state tourism office says you are most likely to find on a grocery shelf, and the one most of the country means by barbecue sauce. The four-sauce map gives it the western and northwestern corner of South Carolina: Greenville, Spartanburg, Anderson, Greenwood, the Savannah River side. Hash here is often beef, or pork and beef with onions, over rice.

name: Light tomato barbecue
what: Pork — whole hog in the Pee Dee, shoulders and hams in the upper Midlands — cooked over coals or on cookers and served with a thin sauce that is the Carolinas' vinegar-and-pepper with ketchup stirred in. On South Carolina's four-sauce map, as the state tourism office and the South Carolina Barbeque Association publish it, it holds the Pee Dee and the upper middle of the state along the North Carolina line. Hash comes with it, of beef as often as pork toward the Upstate. It is the South Carolina twin of Lexington's dip, and the Barbeque Association's history maps the North Carolina Piedmont and the South Carolina Pee Dee as one light-tomato country.

name: South Carolina mustard barbecue
aliases: Midlands barbecue|mustard-based barbecue|Carolina Gold barbecue|Dutch Fork barbecue
what: Pork — whole hogs at some pits, hams or shoulders at others — cooked over hardwood coals or on cookers, chopped or pulled, and dressed with a yellow sauce of prepared mustard, vinegar, sugar and spices. Hash, a stew of pork and onions that in the Midlands often takes mustard too, comes over white rice beside it, and the meal is often a buffet. The style belongs to the Midlands, the counties around Columbia: a belt the geographers Charles Kovacik and John Winberry drew in 1987 from Newberry and Lexington counties down through Orangeburg toward Charleston, the German-settled country whose fork of the Saluda and Broad rivers is called the Dutch Fork.

name: Pee Dee whole-hog barbecue
aliases: Pee Dee barbecue|vinegar-and-pepper barbecue|Williamsburg County barbecue|South Carolina whole hog
what: Whole hogs cooked overnight over hardwood coals, pulled or chopped, and dressed with a thin sauce of vinegar, salt, black pepper and red pepper — the same sauce as eastern North Carolina's across the state line. The skin is taken off and fried into skins sold by the bag. Hash over rice, chicken bog, slaw and white bread fill the plate, often from a buffet. The style belongs to the Pee Dee, the northeast of South Carolina along the Pee Dee and Black rivers — Hemingway, Kingstree, Manning, Florence — and runs down the coast, where the state tourism office marks vinegar-and-pepper as the sauce of the shore.

name: Bone Suckin' Sauce
aliases: Bone Suckin' Sweet Southern|Ford's Foods sauce
what: A Raleigh line of bottled sauces, of which the one that built the brand is Sweet Southern: cane sugar first, tomato puree second, water third, apple cider vinegar fourth, at six grams of sugar to the tablespoon. The house also bottles an Eastern Vinegar sauce, whose label puts apple cider vinegar and distilled vinegar first and tomato paste sixth, and a mustard whose seven ingredients name no tomato at all. One maker, three readings of the same state's shelf.

name: Carolina Treet
aliases: Carolina Treet Cooking Barbecue Sauce|Carolina Treet Original
what: A Wilmington sauce that fits none of the four Carolina bases. Its label reads water, vinegar, wheat flour, salt, soybean oil, paprika, garlic, onion, xanthan gum, spices — no tomato, no mustard, no sugar. The wheat flour does what tomato paste does elsewhere: it thickens. What it tastes of is vinegar, smoke and salt, and it carries 536 milligrams of sodium in a tablespoon, the highest figure among the sixty-eight bottles this project measured. The bottle calls itself a cooking barbecue sauce, meaning it goes on during the cook rather than at the table.

name: George's Barbecue Sauce
what: A bottled sauce from Nashville, North Carolina, a Nash County town on the edge of the Coastal Plain, sold in three strengths: Original, Hot and Special. The Original's label reads vinegar, water, tomato concentrate, tomato paste, sugar, apples, salt, high fructose corn syrup, corn syrup, red pepper and spices — vinegar leading, tomato third and fourth, and a sweetening that runs to three separate entries. It carries 3.5 grams of sugar in a tablespoon and 180 milligrams of sodium. The Special reverses the first four: tomato concentrate and tomato paste come before the water and the vinegar, and jalapenos join the list.

name: Golding Farms Foods
what: A Winston-Salem sauce manufacturer, the second of that city's two, and one whose output mostly reaches a table under someone else's name. It sells a retail line under the Golding Farms label — the Honey Mustard dipping sauce reads distilled vinegar, canola oil, sugar, honey, water, mustard seed, at 3.5 grams of sugar to the tablespoon — and blends and packs sauces for brands, food service and industrial customers.

name: heavy tomato sauce
aliases: tomato-and-sugar sauce|sweet red sauce|thick tomato barbecue sauce|Kansas City-style sauce
what: A thick red sauce built on tomato — ketchup, paste or sauce — sweetened with brown sugar or molasses, soured with vinegar and seasoned with spices, cooked down until it clings. It is the sauce of the western and northwestern corner of South Carolina on the state's four-sauce map: the tourism office's 'tomato-and-sugar sauce', the one it says you are most likely to find on a grocery shelf. It goes on after cooking — on the plate, on the bun, on ribs and chicken — and sits on the meat rather than soaking in.

name: Lexington dip
aliases: dip|Lexington-style sauce|Piedmont sauce|Western sauce|red sauce|barbecue dip
what: The Piedmont's sauce: the east's vinegar, salt, pepper and red pepper with ketchup or tomato and water added, sometimes sugar, so that it comes out thin and reddish — tangy, a little sweet or hot by the house, and every restaurant's recipe its own. It is the sauce of pork-shoulder barbecue in Lexington, Greensboro, Salisbury, Shelby and the rest of the Piedmont. It is basted on the shoulders as they cook, goes on the chopped meat at the block, stands on the table, and, in place of mayonnaise, dresses the red slaw.
root: English dip (n.), from the verb dip, Old English dyppan, Proto-Germanic *daupejanan, a causative of *deup- 'deep'. The noun 'act of dipping' is recorded from the 1590s and the sense 'a liquid into which something is dipped' by 1825.

name: light tomato sauce
aliases: light-tomato barbecue sauce|vinegar-and-ketchup sauce|thin red sauce
what: Vinegar-and-pepper sauce with ketchup added — enough to redden and sweeten it a little, not enough to thicken it — and often cayenne or a bottled hot sauce. The state tourism office's description is the whole recipe: 'a vinegar-and-pepper sauce with ketchup added for a little sweetness'. It is the sauce of South Carolina's Pee Dee and upper Midlands on the state's four-sauce map, and the same idea as the Lexington dip across the line, which the South Carolina Barbeque Association counts as the same sauce. It goes on chopped pork at the block and stands on the table.

name: Maurice's Southern Gold
aliases: Southern Gold BBQ Sauce|Maurice's Gourmet Blend|Carolina Gold (former name)
what: The mustard sauce of Maurice's Piggie Park at West Columbia, sold in bottles, half gallons and gallons alongside the family's Hickory Red, Vinegar and Hot Pepper sauces. It is the bottle that carried the South Carolina mustard sauce onto national supermarket shelves in the 1990s, then off them again in 2000. No ingredient list or Nutrition Facts panel is published for it, so this page can name the sauce and its history but cannot measure it.

name: Melvin's Golden Sauce
aliases: Melvin's Original Golden Secret|Golden Secret Sauce
what: The mustard sauce of Melvin's Bar-B-Que in Charleston, sold in 16-ounce glass bottles, half gallons and gallons, beside the house's Southern Red, Sweet Red and Vinegar sauces. The maker publishes no ingredient list and no Nutrition Facts for any of the four, so what this page can give is the history the family tells and the shape of its line, not a measurement.

name: mustard-based barbecue sauce
aliases: Carolina Gold|South Carolina mustard sauce|yellow sauce|gold sauce|Southern Gold (Maurice's)
what: Prepared yellow mustard thinned with vinegar and sweetened with sugar or brown sugar, with black and red pepper and whatever else the house keeps to itself — Bessinger's bottled version listed mustard, brown sugar, soy sauce and vinegar. It is yellow to gold, pourable, sweet-sour with a mustard bite. It belongs to the Midlands of South Carolina, the belt of German-settled counties from Newberry and Lexington through Orangeburg toward Charleston, and is the sauce the state is known for elsewhere. It goes on chopped or pulled pork at the block, is basted on whole hogs at some pits, and goes into hash.
root: Carolina Gold: Maurice Bessinger's supermarket brand name for his mustard sauce, from the sauce's colour and the state. 'Carolina Gold' is also the name of the Lowcountry's rice variety, popularised in South Carolina in the 1780s and named for the golden colour of its unhulled grain; the sauce and the rice are unrelated, and the rice's name is the older by two centuries.

name: Sam Jones BBQ sauce
aliases: Sam Jones Sweet BBQ Sauce|Sam Jones Vinegar
what: A bottled line from the whole-hog house Sam Jones opened at Winterville in 2015, third generation of the Skylight Inn family at Ayden. The Sweet bottle's Nutrition Facts give 10 grams of total sugars and 210 milligrams of sodium in a 2-tablespoon serving, which is 5 grams of sugar and 105 milligrams of sodium to the tablespoon, but the record carries no ingredient list, so its order cannot be read and its base is recorded as other.

name: Scott's Barbecue Sauce
aliases: Scott's Famous Barbecue Sauce|Adam Scott's sauce|Scott's of Goldsboro
what: A bottled eastern North Carolina sauce — vinegar-based, the recipe kept secret, sold as sugar-free and fat-free — made by the Scott family of Goldsboro since the mid-1940s from a recipe the Rev. Adam Scott, a Black Holiness minister who began selling barbecue there in 1917, said came to him in a dream. His son A. Martel Scott Sr. patented it in 1946. The North Carolina Arts Council's trail page calls it 'believed to be the oldest commercially available barbecue sauce in the country'. It is sold in Harris Teeter and Food Lion and from the family's website, and the label offers it for meats, seafood, poultry and vegetables.

name: Texas Pete
aliases: Texas Pete Hot Sauce|Texas Pete Original
what: A cayenne-pepper hot sauce made by the T.W. Garner Food Company of Winston-Salem, North Carolina, since 1929 — mild as hot sauces go, 747 on the Scoville scale — in a flip-top bottle with a red cowboy on a white-and-yellow label. It is not a barbecue sauce and is on this list because of where it stands: on the table at eastern North Carolina barbecue houses beside the vinegar, and, at Skylight Inn in Ayden, in the dressing itself, where the chopped hog is seasoned with vinegar, salt, pepper and Texas Pete.
root: Texas + Pete: 'Texas' for a state known for hot food, chosen over a marketing adviser's 'Mexican Joe' because Sam Garner wanted an American name; 'Pete' was the nickname of his son Harold Garner.

name: vinegar-and-pepper sauce
aliases: eastern sauce|Eastern North Carolina sauce|East Carolina sauce|pepper vinegar|vinegar sauce
what: Vinegar — cider or white — with salt, black pepper and crushed red pepper, and nothing else in its plainest form; some houses add sugar, a bottled hot sauce or lemon. It is thin enough to pour, tart, and as hot as the cook likes. It is the sauce of whole-hog barbecue on the Coastal Plain of both Carolinas, from Rocky Mount to the Pee Dee and the coast: used as a mop while the hog cooks, tossed through the chopped meat at the block, and set on the table for more. Wikipedia's history of barbecue sauce calls it the earliest American barbecue sauce and the root of most of the others.

name: Wells Hog Heaven Barbecue Sauce
what: A vinegar-based sauce made at Burgaw, the seat of Pender County in southeastern North Carolina, and sold in that corner of the state. The maker gives no ingredient list and no Nutrition Facts on its site, so what is on record is the description rather than the measurement: a vinegar sauce for seasoning chopped and pulled pork.

name: baked beans
what: White beans — navy or pea beans — cooked slow in a sweet brown sauce of molasses or brown sugar with pork in it, and served hot in a cup or a compartment of the tray. On a Carolina barbecue plate they usually come from a large can, warmed and doctored at the pit with more sugar, mustard, onion or a handful of chopped barbecue; the traditional form is dried beans parboiled and then baked for hours in a covered pot, and the canned form is cooked through steam rather than baked at all. They belong to the pig pickin' — the outdoor party where guests pull the meat off a whole hog — as much as to the counter.

name: banana pudding
what: Layers of sweet vanilla custard, vanilla wafers and sliced bananas built up in a dish and topped with meringue or whipped cream, then chilled until the wafers soften and the layers run together. It is the barbecue house's dessert in both Carolinas, whole-hog pits and shoulder pits alike: the Barbecue Center in Lexington sells it by the small or large cup, Sam Jones BBQ lists it beside the whole hog, Sweatman's in Holly Hill serves it after hash and rice, and Rodney Scott's in Charleston listed it with the catfish and ribs. It needs no oven, scales up to a crowd and keeps — one theory of how a dessert with no early Southern tie became Southern.

name: barbecue chicken
what: Half a chicken, cooked on the pit beside the pig or on its own cooker until the skin chars, brushed with the house sauce — vinegar and pepper in the east, a thin tomato-and-vinegar dip in the Piedmont — and sold by the half or the whole bird. At eastern pits it is the one other meat: B's in Greenville sells out of chicken halves by early afternoon, and Skylight Inn lists it beside the whole hog. Keaton's in Cleveland, Rowan County, does it the other way round, frying the chicken and dipping it in a hot vinegar-tomato barbecue sauce. NCpedia notes that North Carolinians seldom use 'barbecue' alone for chicken.

name: barbecue sandwich
aliases: chopped barbecue sandwich|barbecue with slaw|Lexington barbecue sandwich|pork sandwich|a barbecue
what: Chopped pork on a soft white bun with slaw laid on the meat. In North Carolina it is the commonest form of the sandwich: whole-hog barbecue dressed with vinegar and pepper in the east, chopped or sliced shoulder with dip and red slaw in the Piedmont. In South Carolina the meat is pulled or chopped and the sauce is mustard, vinegar-pepper or tomato by region, with slaw a common topping. The bun is a plain hamburger roll — at Skylight Inn a white bread roll — and the bread keeps the meat warm and catches the sauce.

name: barbecue tray
aliases: tray|barbecue plate|plate|large tray|chopped tray|sliced tray|coarse chopped tray
what: The unit of ordering at a Carolina barbecue counter: a paper boat or a plate with the chopped pork on one side and slaw on the other, and no bun. In Lexington the meat is pork shoulder and the order names the cut — chopped, coarse chopped (small chunks) or sliced — and the size, tray or large tray; in the east it is whole hog, and the tray or plate carries white slaw with cornbread, a corn stick or hushpuppies. A plate adds french fries and a choice of hushpuppies or rolls. A sandwich is the same meat and slaw on a bun.

name: Blenheim Ginger Ale
what: A ginger ale bottled at Hamer, in Dillon County, South Carolina, made with Jamaica ginger and sugar in mineral water from a spring in Marlboro County, and hot enough that the heat is the point of it. It comes in three strengths: #3 Hot with a pink cap, #5 Not As Hot with a gold cap, and #9 Diet with a white cap. It was made first as a stomach tonic rather than a soft drink, and it sits on Pee Dee barbecue tables the way Cheerwine sits on Piedmont ones.
root: named for Blenheim, Marlboro County, South Carolina, the town that grew up around the mineral spring the drink was first mixed with

name: boiled potatoes
what: Potatoes boiled whole or in halves until they are soft and served beside chopped whole hog on the eastern North Carolina plate — the side the Piedmont does not have. At Parker's in Wilson and, by Bob Garner's account, most eastern restaurants they are stewed rather than plainly boiled: peeled potatoes, often with onion, simmered in water with ketchup or red sauce, hot sauce, paprika, sugar, salt, pepper and a spoon of bacon grease, so the broth seasons them through. They come on the plate with slaw and the plate's bread, a corn stick or hushpuppies, and they have been there since Melton's in Rocky Mount charged 45 cents for barbecue with boiled potatoes in 1929.

name: Brunswick stew
what: A thick tomato stew of chicken or pork with corn, butter beans (lima beans), onion and, in the east, potatoes, cooked in big pots and served in a cup beside the barbecue. Virginia and Georgia both claim it; North Carolina makes it without argument at barbecue houses, church suppers and fundraisers, where it holds the place that hash holds in South Carolina. The name is a county in Virginia or a city in Georgia, both named for the German duchy of Brunswick. The squirrel of the first recipes has given way to chicken, and at a barbecue house some of the chopped pork goes into the pot.

name: Cheerwine
what: A cherry-flavoured soft drink — burgundy-red, sweet, with a strong black-cherry note and more carbonation than most sodas — made in Salisbury, Rowan County, North Carolina by the Carolina Beverage Corporation since 1917, and run by founder L.D. Peeler's family throughout. On a Piedmont barbecue counter it is the soda beside the tea: Lexington Barbecue lists Cheerwine and Diet Cheerwine with the Cokes, and the Barbecue Center sells it by the 10-, 16- and 32-ounce cup. It is bottled in glass with cane sugar as Retro or 'Original 1917 Formula' Cheerwine, comes as ice cream and sherbet in Food Lion, and has had its own festival in Salisbury each year since its centennial in 2017.
root: cheer + wine: named, the company says, for its burgundy-red colour and cheery disposition — wine for the colour, cheer for the taste; it contains no alcohol

name: chicken bog
what: Chicken, rice and smoked sausage cooked together in the chicken's own broth until the rice has taken up the liquid and sits wet and plump — a pilau (rice cooked in stock) that is deliberately wetter than a pilau. It belongs to the Pee Dee, the northeast of South Carolina from Horry County west to Florence, and to the Lowcountry beyond it; Loris, a town of about two thousand north of Myrtle Beach, has held a Bog-Off cook-off every October since 1979. The pot is a fifty-gallon wash pot and the dish is cooked for crowds: tobacco crews, church suppers, the stump meeting at Galivants Ferry.
root: English bog 'wet, soft, spongy ground', c. 1500, from Gaelic and Irish bogach 'bog', from bog 'soft, moist'; applied to the dish for its wet rice

name: collards
what: Broad flat leaves of a loose-headed cabbage, stripped from the stem, cut in ribbons and stewed a long time with a piece of smoked pork until they are dark and soft, in a salty broth the South calls pot liquor. They are a staple of Southern cooking and one of the vegetables a Carolina barbecue buffet is judged by; cornbread is used to soak up what is left in the bowl. Eaten with black-eyed peas and cornbread on New Year's Day for wealth in the year to come.

name: cornbread
what: A quick bread of cornmeal — meal, water or buttermilk, salt, fat, often egg and soda — baked in a pan, a skillet or a stick mould. It comes with eastern North Carolina barbecue in two forms. At the Skylight Inn in Ayden it is a flat, dense cake of stone-ground cornmeal, water, salt and the day's hog drippings, spread thin on a sheet pan, baked and cut in squares; Our State calls it more grit cake than bread. At Parker's, B's, Bum's and a third of the pits in six Coastal Plain counties it is the corn stick, an eight-inch baton of meal, fat and boiling water, baked, then deep-fried. West of the Coastal Plain the bread is hushpuppies.
root: corn (American English for maize) + bread. The bread is Native American in origin — the Hidatsa call baked cornbread naktsi, the Choctaw bvnaha — and the English name is the settlers' description of it

name: Duke's mayonnaise
what: A bottled mayonnaise made in Mauldin, South Carolina, outside Greenville: egg yolks, oil and cider vinegar, with more yolk than most brands and no added sugar, which is where the tang comes from that the company sells it on. In the Carolinas it is the jar a white slaw, a potato salad, a deviled egg, a pimento cheese and a tomato sandwich are made with, and it is the third-largest mayonnaise brand in the United States, behind Hellmann's and Kraft, after a long stretch when it was sold mostly in the South.
root: the founder's married surname: Eugenia Thomas Slade Duke of Greenville, South Carolina, who put her own name on the sandwiches she sold from 1917

name: fried okra
what: Okra pods sliced into rounds, rolled in cornmeal and fried until the outside is crisp. It is the commonest way okra is cooked in the South and a standing side at barbecue houses and meat-and-three counters, eaten most in summer when the pods are in. Cutting the pods small keeps the outside crisp and leaves the inside slippery; whole pods can be fried too.

name: green beans
what: Whole or broken pods of the common bean, stewed slow with a piece of pork until they give up their squeak and take on the meat's salt, and served in a cup or a compartment beside the barbecue. They are the plain vegetable on a Carolina barbecue plate — a house that keeps one vegetable and no buffet usually keeps these — and the Southern way with them is long cooking rather than short, so the pod goes soft and olive rather than staying bright.
root: green + bean; the older Southern names are string beans, for the fibre pulled off the pod before cooking, and snaps, for the sound the pod makes when broken

name: hash and rice
aliases: hash|barbecue hash|South Carolina hash|pork hash|liver hash|liver and lights hash|hash on rice
what: A thick stew, or gravy, of pork cooked down with onions until it can be eaten with a spoon, ladled over white rice beside the barbecue. It is South Carolina's side the way Brunswick stew is Georgia's, Virginia's and North Carolina's, and it is barely known outside the state. The old hash was made from what the whole hog left after the barbecue — the head, the liver and the lights (the lungs) — simmered for a day in an iron pot; most restaurants now use shoulder or ham. Three loose regions: mustard in the Midlands, vinegar and liver in the Lowcountry, beef and onions in the Upstate.
root: French hacher 'to chop up' (from Old French hache 'axe') → English hash, verb, 1650s, 'to hack, chop into small pieces' → hash, noun, 1660s, 'a stew of meat cut into small pieces'

name: hushpuppies
what: Balls or fingers of cornmeal batter — meal, a little flour, egg, buttermilk or water, salt, soda, often onion — dropped by the spoonful into hot oil and fried until the outside is crisp and dark gold and the inside soft and steaming. In the Carolinas they are the bread of the fish fry and, since the 1940s, of the barbecue tray: Lexington pits serve them with the shoulder and red slaw in place of rolls, and most eastern pits give them with whole hog, though a third of the pits in the Wilson–Greenville counties give corn sticks instead. Sweeter and lighter than a corn stick, and fried, not baked.
root: hush + puppy. 'Hush puppy' was slang for something that keeps a thing quiet — hush money in a 1738 British account of smuggling, and from 1879 the gravy or pot liquor that kept the hounds from growling, meaning a growling stomach — and was applied to deep-fried cornmeal by 1899; current in Georgia by 1927 (Moss)

name: mac and cheese
what: Macaroni in a cheese sauce, most often cheddar, baked in a dish until the top browns. On a Carolina barbecue buffet it sits with the vegetables and is taken as one, cut in squares from a hotel pan rather than spooned; a stovetop version bound with a white sauce is the other common form. In the Lowcountry and in Black Southern kitchens the baked, custard-set kind is often called macaroni pie.

name: outside brown
what: The dark crust from the outside of a pork shoulder — the bark, where ten hours of smoke and dip have cooked into the surface — ordered by name at Lexington pits. Regulars ask for extra outside brown on a tray or sandwich; ordered 'brown', the meat comes chopped from that crust rather than from the pale inside. The word marks the Piedmont. Eastern pits chop the whole hog together, skin and all, and have no order for it, though NCpedia notes that some North Carolinians follow South Carolina in separating skin, the dry 'outside meat' and the juicier 'inside meat'.

name: peach cobbler
what: Sliced peaches sweetened and thickened in a deep dish and covered with a crust — pastry, biscuit dough or a batter — then baked until the top browns and the fruit bubbles at the edge. It is a barbecue dessert of the same family as banana pudding, ordered by the cup or the square after the tray, and served warm, often with ice cream. The Southern kind is frequently closer to a deep-dish pie, with a bottom crust as well as a top.

name: pickles
what: Cucumbers held in brine or vinegar until they sour, sliced into rounds or spears and put on the plate beside the meat, with the sandwich, or loose in a dish on the table. Sweet pickle — cucumbers in a vinegar-and-sugar syrup with spices — is the common Carolina one; chow-chow, a chopped relish of cabbage, green tomato, onion and pepper, does the same job in a spoonful. The point of them on a barbecue plate is acid and salt against fat.

name: pig pickin' cake
aliases: pig pickin cake|pig picking cake|pineapple pig pickin' cake|pea pickin' cake|sunshine cake|mandarin orange cake
what: A layer cake of convenience-food parts: yellow or butter-golden cake mix beaten with eggs, oil and a can of mandarin oranges, juice and all, baked in three eight-inch pans and frosted with a can of crushed pineapple folded into instant vanilla pudding and whipped topping, sometimes with pecans or coconut on top, and served cold. It is North Carolina's barbecue dessert by name — the pig pickin' being the whole-hog party where guests pick the meat off the pig — and it is carried to those parties; Hysmith places it at barbecue restaurants too, though it is a home cake first. Our State calls it an essential companion to any good barbecue, noun not verb.
root: pig pickin' (the whole-hog party, named for picking the meat off the cooked pig) + cake

name: pork skins
what: The pig's hide, cooked until it blisters and cracks. On an eastern whole hog the skin faces up through the night and is turned to the coals at the end to crisp; at Skylight Inn it is chopped into the meat, where the crunch and the salt are part of what 'barbecue' means. Sold on their own, skins are a side or a snack: fresh fried squares with pimento cheese at Sam Jones BBQ, a pork skin sandwich with slaw at Lexington Barbecue. In the Pee Dee the hog is sometimes skinned before cooking and the skin fried on its own. A crackling keeps a little fat and meat under the skin; a rind is skin alone.

name: potato salad
what: Boiled potatoes cut up cold and dressed with mayonnaise, with hard-boiled egg, onion, celery, sweet pickle or relish and often a spoon of yellow mustard that colours the whole bowl. It is served cold beside the barbecue, and in the Carolinas it is the mayonnaise side that answers to the vinegar of the meat. Mustard in the dressing is common enough in South Carolina that a bowl of it can read as the same yellow as the sauce.

name: red slaw
what: Finely chopped green cabbage dressed with vinegar, ketchup, sugar, salt and black pepper — or with the pit's own dip — and no mayonnaise. It is the slaw of Lexington and the Piedmont, red-pink in the boat beside the chopped shoulder, on the sandwich under the meat, and on hot dogs as a relish; it is what the counter means by 'slaw' from Lexington to Shelby. Because it carries no mayonnaise it keeps without refrigeration, which suits an outdoor pit. Across the rest of the state the pale mayonnaise slaw is the default and this one is called barbecue slaw.
root: Dutch koolsla 'cabbage salad' (kool 'cabbage', from Latin caulis, + sla 'salad') → American English coleslaw, 1794 → slaw, the American clipping; 'red' is the Lexington marker for the ketchup or dip in the dressing, against 'white' for mayonnaise

name: sweet tea
what: Black tea brewed strong, sweetened with sugar while hot — so it dissolves, rather than being stirred into a cold glass — and poured over ice. It is the drink of the Carolina barbecue house in both states and every sauce region: sold by the glass, the quart and the gallon, brewed on the stove at Grady's in Dudley, named by Dukes in Orangeburg among the five things people come for, and served, Wikipedia says, wherever whole hog is. Some cooks temper it with a pinch of baking soda against bitterness; lemon is the usual addition. Its presence on a menu is one sign used to tell whether a place counts as the South.

name: white slaw
what: Finely chopped cabbage in a dressing of mayonnaise or whipped salad dressing, sweet and pale: the slaw of eastern North Carolina and of most of South Carolina. It goes on the tray beside the chopped whole hog and on the bun of the sandwich, where its sweetness sets off the vinegar and pepper of the meat. Eastern pits use mayonnaise almost universally; NCpedia lists white or yellow coleslaw among the eastern sides, the yellow taking mustard. The name exists only where the red slaw does. Everywhere else in the state this is coleslaw, from the Dutch koolsla, cabbage salad.

name: block pit
what: An open pit built above ground of cinder blocks — concrete blocks — wide and shallow, a little longer than a split hog, with a rack across the top on which the pig lies and a bed of charcoal below; brick or steel are the alternatives, and the charcoal is made in a fireplace or a burn barrel beside it. It is the whole-hog pit of the Carolinas, the one a farm, a fire department or a family can lay in an afternoon. *Tradition holds —* the blocks go up dry, without mortar, two or three courses high, a gap is left for the shovel, and a sheet of tin or plywood closes the top.

name: brick pit
what: The masonry pit of the Piedmont: a closed brick chamber with a rack for the shoulders and a chimney through the roof to carry off the smoke. Coals made from oak and hickory go in through the door and are spread on the floor under the meat; the door shuts and the shoulders cook nine to twelve hours at about 200 to 225 degrees. The Barbecue Center in Lexington describes its pit as a brick oven with three chambers, 'comparable to an oversized smoker', and Lexington Barbecue's roof carries a row of smoking stacks. The line of chimneys on a Lexington roof is how you know a wood pit from the road.

name: burn barrel
what: A repurposed steel drum — or, at Scott's in Hemingway, two 55-gallon drums welded together — in which logs are burned down to coals: the wood goes in at the top, the coals are pulled out from below and carried by shovel to the pit. It is the coal-maker of the wood pit, the reason a whole hog can sit over a steady bed of coals for twelve hours with no flame under it. Older pit houses use a fireplace for the same job — the Skylight Inn burns its oak and hickory in fireplaces beside the pits — and the barrel is the version anyone can weld.

name: chopping block
what: A thick wooden block and a pair of cleavers, on which cooked pork is turned into barbecue. The whole hog is pulled from the bones onto the block and chopped, skin and all, until the meat is fine enough to hold a thin vinegar sauce; the salt and the sauce go on at the block — at the Skylight Inn, vinegar, salt, pepper and Texas Pete. A Lexington shoulder is chopped fine, chopped coarse into small chunks, or sliced, and at Lexington Barbecue never pulled. Jane and Michael Stern called the sound of cleavers on the block one of the most alluring aspects of whole hog barbecue in the Carolinas.

name: direct heat
aliases: coals under the meat|open-pit|pit-cooked|cooking on coals
what: The Carolina way of putting fire to meat: a bed of hardwood coals directly beneath the hog or the shoulders, with no flame and no separate firebox. The coals are made elsewhere — in a burn barrel or a fireplace — and shoveled in, so the meat sits over glowing charcoal and its own dripping fat rather than in a stream of smoke. The contrast is the offset smoker of Central Texas: a cylinder with a smaller firebox attached at one end, whose burning post-oak fire sends heat and smoke sideways through the chamber past the meat — indirect heat. The whole-hog article, the Mallard Creek church and the Barbecue Center all describe the coals going under the meat.

name: gas and electric cookers
aliases: gas pit|gas cooker|electric cooker|gas-fired pit|smoker oven
what: The cookers most Carolina barbecue is cooked in: steel ovens fired by propane, natural gas or an electric element, with a thermostat and racks, and often a box for wood chips or a log to put smoke on the meat. A gas smoker lights a burner directly under a box of wood or charcoal; an electric one runs a heating element that holds any temperature from a cold smoke to about 275 degrees. New barbecue restaurants mostly open on them and many older ones switched. They cook overnight unattended, hold a set temperature, make no soot and need no one to shovel coals at three in the morning, and they are the machine behind a great deal of what both states call barbecue, sauce and slaw included.

name: hickory and oak
what: The hardwoods of the Carolina pit. Hickory and oak are the woods a Carolina cook burns, usually together and usually burned down to coals before they go under the meat: Lexington pits cook over oak and hickory coals, the Skylight Inn burns oak and hickory logs in fireplaces beside its pits, and Scott's in Hemingway feeds hickory, oak and pecan through the top of a burn barrel. South Carolina's barbecue is smoked over hickory or oak; Lexington's over a hardwood fire, usually hickory. Both are dense, slow-burning and abundant in the eastern forest, and both give the strong smoke that pork carries. Pecan is itself a hickory — Carya illinoinensis — with a sweeter, milder smoke.

name: hog killing
what: The winter slaughter of the farm's hogs, done on the first cold day of autumn or winter, when the meat would keep. In rural North Carolina neighbors gathered before dawn; water was heated with fire-hot stones dropped into barrels; the penned and fattened hogs were killed with knives, bled, scalded, hung on a gambrel — a spreader bar through the hind legs — and scraped clean of hair; the carcasses cooled overnight and were cut up the next day, the hams, sides, shoulders, jowls and heads salted down in the smokehouse. Lard was rendered, the fat cooked down to cracklings, the trim ground for sausage. It is the farm year's pork day, and the social form the pit barbecue grew up beside.

name: pig cooker
what: A steel box on a trailer chassis, long enough for a split hog, with a hinged lid, a grate, and either a row of propane burners underneath or a bed for charcoal: the cooker of the pig pickin', towed to the church lot, the tailgate or the fire station and home again. Carolina Cooker of Micro, North Carolina, builds one of 12-gauge steel with four propane burners on a leaf-spring trailer, listed at $2,599.99 in September 2026; BQ Grills of Elm City builds towable charcoal-and-wood cookers of eighth-inch steel in five- and six-foot lengths at $7,200 to $9,800. The article on the pig pickin' calls the grills 'as varied as the methods of producing them', some homemade, some custom-made.

name: pork shoulder
what: The front leg and shoulder of the pig, sold as one primal — a primal being one of the large first divisions of a carcass — or split in two: the butt, the upper half with the blade bone, and the picnic, the lower arm half, which cured on the bone is a 'picnic ham'. The butt's name is a barrel, not an anatomy. In the North Carolina Piedmont, shoulder is the only cut that counts as barbecue: Lexington pits salt it, lay it over oak and hickory coals for nine to twelve hours, and serve it chopped, coarse chopped or sliced under a red dip. It is darker meat than the loin and stays moist through a long cook, and it is what packers ship when they will not ship a carcass.
root: Boston + butt, a barrel: in colonial and Revolutionary-era New England butchers stored and shipped this shoulder cut in barrels called butts, and the Boston-area method of cutting it gave the cut its name. Picnic (the lower shoulder): cured on the bone it is a 'picnic ham'; no origin for the name is cited here.

name: whole hog
what: The entire dressed pig — dressed meaning gutted and scraped of hair, the head sometimes left on — split open along the backbone, laid flat over coals and cooked as one piece, then pulled from the bones and chopped together: ham, shoulder, loin, belly and, in the Carolinas, the crisped skin. It is the oldest form of open-pit barbecue in the United States and the cut that defines eastern North Carolina and the Pee Dee of South Carolina. A hog of 80 to 120 pounds dressed weight is the usual size for a pig pickin'; restaurants choose small hogs and cook them hot so the skin crisps, and a whole animal can run to 300 pounds.

name: 12 Bones Smokehouse
what: A mountain barbecue house now trading from Hendersonville Road in Arden, south of Asheville, after Hurricane Helene took its River Arts District room in September 2024. Tom Montgomery and Sabra Kelley opened the first one in 2005 in a cinder-block shack on an Asheville floodplain; Bryan and Angela King have owned it since about 2012. Ribs are the signature — blueberry-chipotle and other glazes that are not Carolina orthodoxy — with pulled pork alongside. Barack Obama ate here in April 2010, which is the thing most often said about it.

name: Allen & Son Barbeque
aliases: Allen & Son|Allen and Son Bar-B-Que|Allen & Son Barbecue
what: The hickory-fired pork-shoulder restaurant on Millhouse Road at N.C. 86 north of Chapel Hill that Keith Allen opened in 1971 at nineteen and closed in the first week of December 2018, quietly, to avoid a long goodbye. Allen split the hickory himself, fired the pit every half hour for nine hours, and dressed the chopped shoulder with the hot vinegar sauce he had from his father — an eastern sauce on Piedmont meat. His wife Tammy waited tables for thirty years and made the ice cream; the pies, cobblers and banana pudding were the second reason to come. A separate Allen & Son in Pittsboro, under a licensing agreement, stayed open.

name: Alston Bridges Barbecue
what: The Shelby pork-shoulder house of the other Bridges family, on East Grover Street in Cleveland County, where Alston Bridges and his wife Mabel bought the property in 1955. Alston learned the trade from his brother-in-law Warner Stamey, managing Stamey's Log Cabin Barbecue in Lexington for two and a half years first. About fifty shoulders a day go through the kitchen; the tray is chopped or coarse-chopped pork with red slaw and hushpuppies. What is under the meat is disputed: three accounts describe electric cookers or gas, one promotional listing says wood-smoked.

name: Backyard BBQ Pit
aliases: Backyard Barbecue Pit|The Backyard BBQ Pit
what: A Black-owned barbecue restaurant on N.C. 55, the Apex Highway, in southeast Durham, opened in April 2007 by Fabianne and Melvin Simmons, who bought a struggling restaurant and made it a neighborhood institution: chopped barbecue and sandwiches, ribs, smoked chicken and oxtails, cooked over wood coals and made from scratch. Its later years were hard — a $50,000 GoFundMe in 2023, a change of owners, eight months dark for renovations before a March 2024 reopening, and in April 2026 a report that it was weeks from closing unless a buyer came. Its status in September 2026 is not confirmed on this disk.

name: Bar-B-Q Center
aliases: The Barbecue Center|Barbecue Center|Lexington Barbecue Center
what: A pork-shoulder pit and ice-cream counter on North Main Street in Lexington, Davidson County, that began in 1955 as a dairy bar, put a shoulder on a pit one slow winter, and has been the Conrad family's since: Sonny Conrad (1938–2013), who started on curb service there as a teenager in 1955 and became owner in 1969, his wife Nancy, and their sons Michael and Cecil. Shoulders cook over hickory; the barbecue comes chopped, sliced or 'brown' — the smoky outside of the shoulder — with the dip and red slaw. The ice cream never left: about 200 gallons a week, much of it in a banana split of three and a half pounds.

name: Bessinger's Bar-B-Q
aliases: Bessinger's BBQ|Bessinger's Bar-Be-Que|Bessinger's Barbeque|Piggy Park Drive-In|Bessinger's — The Barbecue Family
what: A Bessinger family barbecue house at 1602 Savannah Highway in Charleston's West Ashley. Thomas Bessinger came from Holly Hill to Charleston with his brother Melvin in 1955, opened his own restaurant in 1960, and in 1961 the brothers opened Piggy Park Drive-In on the highway; renamed Bessinger's in 1971, it is run by Thomas's sons Tommy and Michael. It serves chopped pork in the family's mustard sauce, ribs, hash and rice, and a buffet on weekend evenings, and the South Carolina Barbeque Association lists it as 100-Mile Barbecue — a house worth a hundred-mile drive. It is the Charleston branch of the family whose Columbia branch is Maurice's Piggie Park.

name: Big T Bar-B-Q
what: A Black-owned wood-burning pit on Congaree Road at Gadsden, in lower Richland County below Columbia, run by Larry Brown, known as Teddy and as Big T, who has sold barbecue to the Columbia area for more than thirty years. Logs burn down in a warped burn box behind the smokehouse and the coals are shovelled into low metal pits under pork shoulders. Hash goes over rice, made with pork and offal in the Midlands way. A second house on Garners Ferry Road in Columbia serves the same barbecue from a buffet.

name: Bobbee O's BBQ
what: A Black-owned barbecue counter on Statesville Road in north Charlotte, opened in 2008 by Bob Steven Roberts after four years working on his sauce. The board runs to pulled pork, ribs, brisket and wings rather than whole hog, and the room is counter service with online ordering. Roberts's niece Chloria Chandler is his business partner. It is one of the few barbecue businesses in Mecklenburg County that the Black-owned business directories carry, and the only one in this project's Charlotte records.

name: Bobby's BBQ
what: A Texas-leaning smokehouse on North Main Street in Fountain Inn, Greenville County, owned by Octavius Nelson, called Tay, and his wife Sarah. Brisket, pulled pork, ribs, turkey and house-made sausage come off the pits; there is no hash and no buffet, which sets it apart from most South Carolina barbecue houses. The name is for Tay's father Bobby Nelson Sr. and his brother Bobby Jr., both dead before the business began. A seasoning line came first, in 2010; the restaurant followed.

name: Brown's Bar-B-Que
what: A farm family's buffet house on the Williamsburg County Highway north of Kingstree, in the Pee Dee, opened in 1981 as a take-out window by Thomas M. Brown Jr., a row-crop farmer, with a dining room added about ten years on. Whole hogs are cooked and chopped, mopped on the pit with a vinegar-and-hot-pepper sauce the family calls barbecue gravy, and set on a long buffet with ribs, smoked ham, barbecued and fried chicken, barbecued and baked turkey, perloo, liver hash and rice, and vegetables the Browns grow themselves — corn, squash, okra, butter beans, collards, cabbage. The Barbeque Association names it among the state's top barbecue houses.

name: B's Barbecue
what: A whole-hog and chicken pit on the edge of Greenville, Pitt County, in a converted country store on a road the county named for it. Bill McLawhorn, the B, opened it in 1978 with his wife Peggy; their daughters Judy Drach, Tammy Godley and Donna McLawhorn have run it since his death in 2007. There is no telephone, no take-out menu and no closing time: the doors open at nine in the morning and shut when the day's barbecue and chicken are gone, usually early afternoon. Cash or check only. The line forms before opening.

name: Bum's Restaurant
what: A wood-fired whole-hog restaurant in downtown Ayden, Pitt County, opened in 1963 by Latham 'Bum' Dennis, of the family that counts Skilton Dennis's 1830 wagon as the start of barbecue for sale here, and run by his son Larry, who cuts the wood, burns the coals and starts around four in the morning. Unlike most eastern pits it keeps a buffet of vegetables cooked that day — collards from the family garden, cabbage pastry, stewed rutabaga, black-eyed peas, boiled potatoes — beside the chopped barbecue. The sign is modest; the smell does the advertising.

name: Buxton Hall Barbecue
what: A whole-hog restaurant that ran from August 2015 to November 22, 2023 in a 1930s roller rink on Banks Avenue in Asheville's South Slope, opened by pitmaster Elliott Moss with Meherwan Irani's Chai Pani restaurant group. Pasture-raised pigs from western North Carolina farms smoked over wood from ten at night to eight in the morning; the plate carried South Carolina hash over rice — the pig's organs and fatty trimmings cooked down to a gravy — beside the chopped hog, with a fried-chicken sandwich, smoked baked beans and pimento cheese, lard-crust pies and banana pudding under meringue. The rink's murals stayed on the walls.

name: Cannon's BBQ
what: A small barbecue house in a converted mobile home at a five-way crossroads in Little Mountain, Newberry County — the Dutch Fork, the German-settled land between the Broad and Saluda rivers where the Midlands mustard sauce is at home. The Cannons cooked over wood coals they burned down themselves and chopped the pork for a sauce with a concentrated yellow-mustard taste; the ribs fell off the bone, and the hash — the Midlands' stew of pork and onion, here tinged bright yellow with mustard — is what Robert Moss remembered it for. It has closed: Moss, writing in March 2020, called it recently closed.

name: Carolina Bar-B-Que
aliases: Carolina BBQ|Carolina Bar-B-Que of New Ellenton
what: A mustard-sauce buffet house on South Main Street in New Ellenton, Aiken County, founded by Willie Mae Walker and her son Jess. She was born Willie Mae Baltzegar, daughter of the Rowesville pitmaster Willie Baltzegar, which puts a pit-cooking line behind the place two generations deep. Pork shoulders cook over wood in smokers out back — not open-pit whole hog. The buffet was twelve dollars in April 2025 and the hash is rust-orange and thick enough to lift on a fork. Thomas Zeigler has run it since about 2022.

name: Clyde Cooper's BBQ
what: Raleigh's downtown barbecue house since New Year's Day 1938, when Clyde Cooper opened on East Davie Street with fifty dollars borrowed from a brother-in-law; it moved around the corner to 327 South Wilmington Street in 2014 when the old building was lost to development, carrying the awning and the front door with it. It cooks pork shoulders — hand-trimmed, never whole hog — in pits on the upper floor, chops them and dresses them with Cooper's tangy sauce, which the city's tourism office calls a blend of eastern and Lexington ways. Fried chicken, Brunswick stew, collards, hushpuppies, boiled potatoes and banana pudding fill out the board; fried pork skins ride on the tray.

name: Cook's Barbecue
what: A pork-shoulder pit off Valiant Drive south of Lexington, Davidson County, built by hand in 1969 by Doug Cook on a cul-de-sac plot down the road from his house — a pit and kitchen, a wooden chopping block, a drive-up window — with a dining room he framed from oaks felled on the lot. His son Brandon, born a year after the restaurant, came back as pitmaster in 2001 and kept the original brick pit and the hickory coals. In an October report DavidsonLocal recorded that the restaurant, by then trading as Cooks & BBQ Still Smoking, had announced on July 28 that it was closed indefinitely and would be sold; no reopening is on this disk.

name: Cooper's Country Store
what: A whitewashed general store on US 521 near Salters, south of Kingstree in Williamsburg County, that sells hardware, groceries, gasoline, diesel, propane, plow points, cast-iron cookware, live crickets — and, from a small meat counter at the back, whole-hog barbecue cooked over wood embers, hash, boiled peanuts and salt-cured country hams. Theron Burrows opened it as an Esso station in 1937; George Cooper built the pit after 1974; his nephew Russell Cooper has run it since 2003. It is a store, not a restaurant, and the barbecue is one more thing it keeps.

name: Dukes Bar-B-Que
aliases: Dukes|Duke's Bar-B-Que|Dukes Bar-B-Que Whitman|Dukes Bar-B-Que Chestnut
what: The name on a dozen or more buffet houses across the Midlands and Lowcountry, all descended from the sons of Manuel Dukes of Orangeburg County, who learned pit cooking from a Rowesville pitmaster and catered the county's gatherings. In Orangeburg itself the line is Earl Duke's: he opened downtown at Chestnut Street and Columbia Road in 1955 and later moved to Whitman Street, and his sister's family runs a second Dukes on Chestnut Street. Both sell from a buffet line: chopped pork in a mustard-and-ketchup 'rust' sauce, hash over rice — the Midlands' stew of pork and onion — fried and barbecued chicken, and a loaf of sliced white bread at the end.

name: Fuzzy's Bar-B-Q
what: A pork-shoulder house on Highway Street in Madison, Rockingham County, opened in 1954 by T.H. 'Fuzzy' Nelson and in the Nelson family since. Shoulders cook over hickory coals in pits behind the building; the tray is the Piedmont tray, chopped or coarse-chopped pork with the dip — the thin vinegar-and-ketchup sauce of the region — red slaw and hushpuppies. It holds True 'Cue certification, which turns on wood or charcoal being the only heat under the meat, and it is a stop on the North Carolina Barbecue Society's Historic Barbecue Trail. Breakfast is served from early morning, which few barbecue houses do.

name: Grady's Barbecue
what: A whole-hog pit at a country crossroads in Dudley, Wayne County, south of Goldsboro, opened on July 4, 1986 by Steve and Gerri Grady and run by Gerri and their son Scottie since Steve's death in August 2025. Hogs cook over oak and hickory coals; the barbecue is chopped by hand and served with stewed collards, cabbage, slaw and potato salad, and tea Gerri brews on the stove. The Assembly reported in February 2026 that it is, by most accounts, the one Black-owned brick-and-mortar whole-hog restaurant at the top of North Carolina's best-of lists, and one of the last of its kind. It opens four days a week.

name: Henry's Smokehouse
what: An Upstate barbecue house at 240 Wade Hampton Boulevard on the edge of downtown Greenville, opened by Beau Hammond — in 1991 by the company's own account, in 1992 by the Greenville Journal's — in a small building that had been other eateries before. It cooks pork butts twelve hours and ribs six to eight over hickory logs in open pits, hand-pulls and chops the pork, and serves it with two sauces, a mild tomato-based one in the Piedmont manner and a spicy mustard one, with hash and rice on the side. A second house is in Simpsonville and a food truck, Henry's Hog Hauler, travels; the Barbeque Association lists it as 100-Mile Barbecue.

name: Hite's Bar-B-Que
what: A take-out barbecue stand on Dreher Road in West Columbia, open only on Friday and Saturday, where the Hite family has cooked whole hogs and hams over oak and hickory coals since 1957. It sells chopped pork, ham, ribs, pork skins, chicken, hash and rice and slaw by the plate and the pound, with a yellow mustard sauce applied lightly; there is no dining room, only picnic tables by a pond. The hash — the Midlands' stew of pork and onion — is made in cast-iron kettles over wood embers. It is not Jackie Hite's of Batesburg-Leesville, some twenty-five miles west, which closed in 2018.

name: Home Team BBQ
aliases: Fiery Ron's Home Team BBQ|Home Team
what: A Charleston barbecue company that began in November 2006 when Aaron Siegel, a Culinary Institute-trained cook from Atlanta, turned Bunch's, a mid-century gas station at 1205 Ashley River Road in West Ashley, into Fiery Ron's Home Team BBQ. It cooks pulled pork, ribs, brisket and smoked chicken wings with an Alabama white sauce, runs a bar known for American whiskey and frozen drinks — the Game Changer is its signature — and books live Americana, blues and bluegrass. Seven locations by 2026: West Ashley, Sullivan's Island (2009), downtown Charleston (2016), Aspen (2016), Columbia (2019), Greenville (2021) and north Mount Pleasant (2022), with more than six hundred employees.

name: Hursey's Bar-B-Q
what: The Burlington, Alamance County, barbecue business of the Hursey family: Sylvester and Daisy Hursey began smoking pork over a backyard pit in 1945 with a sauce of their own, moved to a cafe in Gibsonville with two big pits behind it, and built a Burlington restaurant on Rauhut Street in 1957; their son Charles took over the Burlington trade in 1966, and his sons Chuck and Chris manage it now, a fourth generation coming on. It smokes more than 1,200 pork shoulders a week over hickory, plus hams, for five restaurants, a catering house and a wholesale trade; broasted chicken and hot apple turnovers are the other things it is known for.

name: Jack Cobb & Son Barbecue Place
aliases: Jack Cobb & Son|Jack Cobb and Son Barbecue
what: A Black-owned whole-hog counter on South Main Street in Farmville, Pitt County, that Jack Cobb and his son Rudy built as a cinder-block storefront in 1971 and closed in the autumn of 2018. Hogs cooked all night over oak, pecan and hickory coals banked around them; Rudy Cobb shovelled glowing coals in from the hearth and would not use gas. There were no chairs and no tables, only a counter, three days a week. Barbecued chicken and barbecued turkey shared the board with the pork.

name: Jackie Hite's Bar-B-Q
aliases: Jackie Hite's Bar-B-Que|Jackie Hite's BBQ|Jackie Hite's
what: A whole-hog buffet house on East Railroad Avenue in Leesville, across the tracks from the town, that James Lee 'Jackie' Hite opened in May 1979 and ran until his death in September 2016; his family closed it in 2018. Hogs cooked whole over hickory coals, the coals made in a burn barrel — a steel drum in which the logs burn down — and the chopped meat was dressed with a mustard, vinegar and pepper sauce and set on a buffet with fried chicken, hash and rice, collards, field peas and creamed corn, paid for on the way out. Hite was also Leesville's mayor and fire chief.

name: Keaton's Barbecue
what: A chicken house in the crossroads community of Cleveland, Rowan County, west of Salisbury, where since 1953 the chicken has been fried (or baked) and then dipped whole in a hot vinegar-and-tomato barbecue sauce — 'dipped chicken', a North Carolina barbecue of its own kind. Burette Walker 'B.W.' Keaton, a Black railroad man laid off in 1953, started it in a shack and turned down moves to Statesville and Charlotte; he died in 1989, and his niece Kathleen Murray has run it since 1991. Half or whole, white or dark, hot or mild, with a slice of white bread and a hot vinegar slaw.

name: Kepley's Bar-B-Q
what: A High Point, Guilford County, barbecue stand in a surplus World War II Quonset hut — a half-cylinder of corrugated steel — opened in June 1948 by Hayden Kepley on North Main Street and closed on February 8, 2025 after 77 years. Bob Burleson came to work there as a sixteen-year-old curb boy the year it opened, bought it with Charlie Johnson when Kepley retired in 1962, and ran it until his death in May 2022 at ninety; his daughter Susan Burleson closed it when she could not staff the hours. It served chopped, vinegary pork with tangy red slaw on a bun, hushpuppies, and 85-cent coffee with refills.

name: Lewis Barbecue
what: A Central Texas-style barbecue restaurant at 464 North Nassau Street on the upper peninsula of Charleston, opened in June 2016 by John Lewis, a pitmaster from El Paso who cooked in Austin with Franklin Barbecue and then as a partner in La Barbecue, welding his own smokers along the way. The meat is sold by the pound from a counter: prime brisket, beef ribs, pork spare ribs, turkey breast, pulled pork, 'Texas hot guts' sausage and a green-chile cheddar sausage, with sides from Texas — pinto beans, green chile corn pudding — and from here, collards. A second Lewis opened in Greenville in August 2022 and a third in Atlanta in December 2025.

name: Lexington Barbecue
what: The pork-shoulder pit on Smokehouse Lane in Lexington, Davidson County, that Wayne Monk opened in 1962 at 26 after working under Warner Stamey, and that he owns with his son Rick. Shoulders cook nearly half a day over oak and hickory coals under four brick chimneys whose white smoke shows from the road; the meat is served chopped or sliced with the 'dip', the thin vinegar-and-ketchup sauce of the Piedmont, and with red slaw dressed with the same. Locals call it the Honeymonk, after Monk and his early partner Sonny Hunneycutt. The James Beard Foundation named it an America's Classic in 2003.

name: Luella's Bar-B-Que
what: An Asheville barbecue house on Merrimon Avenue with a second room at Biltmore Park, opened in 2007 by Jeff Miller and named for his grandmother and his daughter. Jeff and Ashley Miller own it. Pork butts, ribs, whole chickens, brisket and turkey come off a smoker that a 2011 account had running hickory coals around the clock; the sauce is the Coastal Plain's vinegar rather than a mountain sweet one. Macaroni and cheese is on the board because the daughter it is half named for likes it.

name: Maurice's Piggie Park BBQ
aliases: Maurice's Piggie Park|Maurice's BBQ|Maurice's Gourmet Barbeque|Piggie Park|Maurice's
what: A chain of eight barbecue restaurants around Columbia run from the original drive-in at 1600 Charleston Highway, West Columbia, where Maurice Bessinger and his brother Joe Jr. opened in 1953. Pork hams cook twenty-four hours over hickory coals at the West Columbia pits and go out daily to the 'Pit-Stop' locations; the meat is served chopped, in sandwiches and plates, with the yellow mustard sauce the company bottles as Southern Gold — sold for decades as Carolina Gold. Maurice's sons Lloyd and Paul, his daughter Debbie and his grandchildren run it. The name also carries a 1968 Supreme Court case and the flag fight of 2000.

name: McCabe's Bar-B-Q
what: A family buffet house on North Brooks Street in Manning, Clarendon County, where the McCabes cook whole hogs, shoulders and hams together for ten to twelve hours over wood coals, on pits David McCabe built in a screened room off the back porch. The pulled meat is mixed and dressed with a vinegar-and-pepper sauce, slightly sweet with a little heat — the Pee Dee's sauce, not the Midlands' mustard — and set out with hash and rice, perloo, fried chicken and a table of vegetables. Open Friday and Saturday middays, cash only, closed for January. Southern Living has listed it among the South's top fifty barbecue houses.

name: Melton's Barbecue
what: The Rocky Mount whole-hog house that Wikipedia records as North Carolina's first sit-down barbecue restaurant. Bob Melton, a horse trader, cooked hogs for friends in an open pit by the Tar River, sold meat by the pound, and in 1924 (some accounts say 1922) opened a shed of a restaurant that grew room by room. It served finely chopped whole hog with a vinegar sauce, boiled potatoes, slaw, corn sticks, hushpuppies and Brunswick stew, and sent barbecue out by bus to parties across the state. Floods from Hurricanes Fran and Floyd drove it out of the river bottom, and it closed in 2005.

name: Melvin's Legendary Bar-B-Que
what: A Charleston mustard-sauce house with rooms on Folly Road on James Island and on Houston Northcutt Boulevard in Mount Pleasant, opened in 1982 by Melvin Bessinger with his son David after Melvin left the partnership with his brother Thomas at Bessinger's. David Bessinger runs it now, and the thing that distinguishes it is a reversal: in 2015 he took out the gas-assisted pits and went back to cooking over wood alone. Pork shoulders go twenty-four hours at about two hundred degrees over smouldering hickory.

name: Midway BBQ
what: A hash house and meat market on Main Street in Buffalo, a mill village in Union County in the Upstate, in business since about 1941 and the last of the nearly fifty hash houses the county once had. Hash here is the Upstate's kind: beef, butter, onion, salt and pepper cooked down slowly in three hundred-gallon pots, sold over rice and by the quart, and it outsells the barbecue three or four to one. The barbecue is hickory-smoked shoulder and ham, chopped; a creamy, spicy chicken stew goes out by the hundred gallons a day; and the front of the building is a butcher's counter with sawdust on the floor.

name: Morris Barbeque
what: A Saturday-only whole-hog house on Morris BBQ Road outside Hookerton, in Greene County, in business since 1956; the county named the road for it. William Morris Jr., grandson of the founder Willie McKinley Morris, cooks the hogs, chops the meat and works the counter. The pig goes on a gas machine built in Wilson in the early 1970s, its burners set off to one side rather than under the meat. Doors open at eight for take-out and half past nine for the dining room, and the barbecue is usually gone by one.

name: Parker's Barbecue
aliases: The Original Parker's Barbecue|Parker's|Parker's BBQ of Wilson
what: A large eastern barbecue house on U.S. 301 south of Wilson, opened in August 1946 by brothers Graham and Ralph Parker and their cousin Henry Parker Brewer, and owned since 1987 by Donald Williams, who started there in 1963, with partners Eric Lippard and Kevin Lamm. It cooks about 150 whole hogs and fries about 8,000 chickens a week for some 20,000 customers, on gas cookers the founders installed in the 1950s. The barbecue is chopped fine and dressed with vinegar and red pepper; young staff in white paper caps seat the room; cash or check only.

name: Red Bridges Barbecue Lodge
aliases: Bridges Barbecue Lodge|Bridges BBQ Lodge|Red Bridges
what: The Shelby, Cleveland County, pork-shoulder house of the Bridges family, begun in 1946 by Red Bridges, an Army cook home from the war, and his wife Lyttle, and run by their daughter Debbie Bridges-Webb with her children Natalie Ramsey, who runs the front, and Chase Webb, who tends the pits overnight. Shoulders cook seven to eight hours a side over hickory and oak — no gas, no electric, the family told WBTV in 2026 — and the recipes are the ones the Bridges started with. The lodge on U.S. 74, across from the Cleveland Mall, marked eighty years in June 2026.

name: Rodney Scott's Whole Hog BBQ
what: A whole-hog restaurant at 1011 King Street on the Charleston peninsula, opened in February 2017 by Rodney Scott of Hemingway and the restaurateur Nick Pihakis in a former fried-chicken house, with seats for about 128, a drive-through and delivery. It cooked whole hogs over hardwood coals and served the pulled pork with a hot vinegar sauce beside spare ribs, fried catfish, a rib-eye sandwich and banana pudding. Sister restaurants followed in Birmingham in 2019 and in Atlanta and a second Alabama town in 2021. Every location closed in May 2026 amid lawsuits and liens against Pihakis's restaurant group, and the King Street doors have stayed shut since.

name: Sam Jones BBQ
aliases: Sam Jones Barbecue|Sam Jones BBQ Winterville|Sam Jones BBQ Raleigh
what: A whole-hog restaurant in Winterville, Pitt County, opened on November 10, 2015 by Sam Jones, grandson of the Skylight Inn's founder Pete Jones, with his partner Michael Letchworth, and a second house in downtown Raleigh since February 2021. Whole hogs are smoked on site over wood, chopped and served daily; the menu runs longer than the Skylight's, with ribs, smoked chicken and turkey, cornbread, slaw and collards, banana pudding, and in Raleigh a full bar. Winterville is seven miles from the Skylight Inn in Ayden; Raleigh is the family's first restaurant outside Pitt County.

name: Scott's Bar-B-Que
aliases: Scott's Variety Store and Bar-B-Q|Scott's Variety Store|Scott's BBQ|Scott's of Hemingway
what: A whole-hog pit behind a country store on the Hemingway Highway in Williamsburg County, in the Pee Dee. Roosevelt and Ella Scott opened the store in 1972 and the barbecue began as a weekend sideline; it grew into the business, and into the pit where their son Rodney Scott learned the trade before he opened his own restaurant in Charleston in 2017. Whole hogs cook eight to twelve hours over coals burned down from hickory, oak and pecan, and the meat is pulled and dressed with a thin sauce of vinegar and pepper. It sells by the plate and the sandwich, cash only, four days a week.

name: Scott's Famous Barbecue
aliases: Scott's Barbecue|Scott's Cafe|Adam Scott's|Scott's Sauce Company
what: The Goldsboro barbecue of the Rev. Adam Scott, a Black cook and preacher who catered barbecues from the 1910s, sold from the back door of his house on Brazil Street from the early 1930s, and whose son A. Martel Scott patented the family's vinegar sauce as Scott's Famous Barbecue Sauce in 1946. The company dates the sauce to 1917 and sells about a million bottles a year. The restaurants — three around Goldsboro by 1950 — are closed: after a first closure in 2001 the family ran on Thursday and Friday lunches for a while, then stopped to make sauce.

name: Shealy's Bar-B-Que
what: A buffet house on East Columbia Avenue in Batesburg-Leesville, Lexington County, opened in June 1969 by Victor and Sara Shealy with their teenage children Tommy and Nancy, and family-run since. It is the barbecue buffet in its fullest form: pork shoulders smoked by the thousand each week and served chopped with mustard sauce — vinegar and tomato sauces alongside — hash over rice, fried chicken, ribs, country-fried steak and more than forty home-cooked sides, with a salad bar and a dessert bar, all you can eat. The South Carolina House marked its fiftieth anniversary with a resolution in 2019.

name: Short Sugar's Pit Bar-B-Q
aliases: Short Sugar's|Short Sugars BBQ|Short Sugar's Drive-In
what: A drive-in barbecue on South Scales Street in Reidsville, Rockingham County, opened in June 1949 by the Overby brothers and named for the one who died two days before the opening, and closed in January 2025 after 75 years. It cooked over hickory coals in two small pits visible from the counter — hams for sliced barbecue, shoulders for chopped — and dressed the meat with a thin dark sauce built on Worcestershire and sugar rather than the ketchup of the Piedmont dips, a sauce that fit neither of North Carolina's camps. Curb service ran to the end.

name: Shuler's Bar-B-Que
what: An all-you-can-eat barbecue house on Highway 38 between Latta and Sellers, in Dillon County in the Pee Dee, opened in 1996 by Norton and Lynn Hughes and named for Norton's father Shuler Hughes, who made the sauce in 1956, and for their grandson of the same name. Pork cooks over wood coals; the buffet runs to more than twenty items and includes liver hash over rice. It is open Thursday to Saturday. The Barbeque Association gives it the hundred-mile designation.

name: Skylight Inn BBQ
aliases: Skylight Inn|Pete Jones' Skylight Inn|the Skylight
what: A whole-hog pit in Ayden, Pitt County, opened by Walter B. 'Pete' Jones on July 8, 1947 and run by his family since. Hogs cook, heads on, over coals burned down from oak and hickory logs; the meat is chopped on a block with the crisp skin chopped through it, dressed with vinegar, salt, pepper and Texas Pete, and served on a tray with slaw and a square of dense cornbread. A wood-and-aluminum copy of the U.S. Capitol dome sits on the roof.

name: Smithfield's Chicken 'N Bar-B-Q
aliases: Smithfield's|SCNB|Smithfield Bar-B-Q|Smithfield's Chicken and Barbeque|Smithfield Chicken & BBQ
what: A quick-service chain of eastern North Carolina barbecue and fried chicken — 41 restaurants across the state as of March 2024, and an online store — begun by Junius and Maggie Moore in downtown Smithfield, Johnston County, in 1977 as Smithfield Bar-B-Q. It sells the eastern pairing over a counter, chopped pork and fried chicken, from the coast to the Triangle, and it stands in Wikipedia's list of the state's notable barbecue restaurants beside Melton's and the Skylight Inn. It is the chain form of the tradition, described here the same way as a wood pit.

name: Speedy Lohr's Barbecue
what: A wood-burning pork house on NC 8 south of Lexington, Davidson County, run by Randy and Amy Lohr, who bought the building in June 2013 from Whitley's Barbecue and carried the family name onto it. Randy's father was Sherman Paul 'Speedy' Lohr, who started the first Speedy's on Highway 52 and learned under Warner Stamey. The pits burn wood and the family says plainly that they always will. The tray is the Piedmont tray, chopped shoulder with the dip and red slaw; pork-skin sandwiches come out on Thursdays.

name: Speedy's Barbecue
what: A Lexington pork-shoulder house that Paul 'Speedy' Lohr opened as a drive-in in 1963 and the Dunn family has run since the early 1970s. Roy and Ella Dunn hold it now. The pork cooks in five electric cookers that look like large rotisserie ovens — not over wood, which is why the house appears on no wood list and on no trail, and which makes it a plain case of how much of the Piedmont cooks. The tray is the Piedmont tray: chopped shoulder, the dip, red slaw, hushpuppies.

name: Stamey's Barbecue
what: The Greensboro pork-shoulder house of the Stamey family, opened by Warner Stamey in 1953 as a drive-in on High Point Road (now West Gate City Boulevard) and run by his grandson Chip since 1993, with a second restaurant on Battleground Avenue. Fifteen-pound shoulders cook eight to ten hours over hickory coals; the barbecue is chopped or sliced and served with the dip, the thin red vinegar sauce of the Piedmont, red slaw and hushpuppies — which the family says Warner Stamey was the first to put beside barbecue in North Carolina. The name reaches back to a Lexington stand of 1938.

name: Stephenson's Bar-B-Q
what: A family barbecue house on N.C. 50 at Willow Spring, in western Johnston County south of Raleigh, opened in July 1958 by hog farmer Paul Stephenson and run since his death by his son Andy. It cooks pork shoulders over hardwood charcoal — whole hogs at the start, shoulders later for leaner meat — and barbecue chicken with a tangy sauce, with hushpuppies and collards from the recipes of Paul's wife Jean, a home-economics teacher. It serves about 600 meals a day and closes on Sundays.

name: Sweatman's Bar-B-Que
what: A whole-hog barbecue house in an old farmhouse on Eutaw Road outside Holly Hill, in Orangeburg County, the mustard belt of the Midlands. Harold 'Bub' Sweatman and his wife Margie opened it in 1977 and it has served two days a week since: Friday and Saturday, pulled pork from whole hogs, ribs, hash over rice — hash being the Midlands' stew of pork and onion — and a spicy-sweet mustard sauce, with pork skins when the hogs give them. The open block pits became gas-and-wood smokers; the buffet that made the name ended after the pandemic; the family sold in 2011, and new owners took over in 2026.

name: Tarheel Q
what: A pork-shoulder pit on US 64 west of Lexington, Davidson County, cooking on brick masonry pits behind the building. Leon and Becky Simmons have owned it since December 2017. Smoke shows from the stacks when wood and pork go on together; the tray is the Piedmont tray, chopped shoulder with the dip, red slaw and hushpuppies, and a weekend pork-and-chicken special ran at $11.95 in April 2026. It carries True 'Cue certification, which turns on wood or charcoal being the only heat under the meat. It is not a stop on the Historic Barbecue Trail.

name: The Fiction Kitchen
what: A vegetarian and vegan restaurant in Raleigh whose menu carries a Southern-style pulled barbecue made without pork, served with the slaw and the sides a Carolina plate expects. Carolina Morrison opened it in 2012 on money raised through Kickstarter, ran it downtown for a decade, and reopened it at Gateway Plaza after a move in 2023. It is in this catalogue because it is one of the ways barbecue is cooked and eaten in North Carolina now, and because it is one of the few places in either state a published list names as LGBTQ-owned.

name: True BBQ
what: A Black-owned pit on D Avenue in West Columbia, opened in 2010 by the brothers Ernest and Milton Zanders after years of selling from street corners and events. The wood-fired pits are visible from the front parking lot. Hash and rice is what the place is known for and what it sells by the pint and the quart alongside pulled pork, ribs, pork chops, brisket and chicken. It is open four days, Thursday to Saturday and no more. A second True BBQ trades in Myrtle Beach.

name: Wilber's Barbecue
what: A whole-hog pit on U.S. 70 east of Goldsboro, Wayne County, opened in 1962 by Wilberdean 'Wilber' Shirley and cooked the same way since: split hogs over oak coals in open pits in a cinder-block cookhouse behind a red-brick restaurant with knotty-pine walls and red-checked tablecloths. It closed in March 2019 over unpaid taxes and reopened in July 2020 under Goldpit Partners, a group of Goldsboro natives who bought it and restored the building. The pork is hand-chopped on oak blocks and seasoned with vinegar and spices; fried chicken, collards, fried okra and hushpuppies come alongside.

name: Adam Scott
what: The Rev. Adam Scott (1890–1983) was a Black cook and Holiness minister in Goldsboro who by his company's date went into the barbecue business in 1917, cooking whole hogs in his back yard and selling chopped pork with a vinegar sauce through the back door; between 1931 and 1933 the house on Brazil Street became a restaurant. He said the sauce came to him in a dream; his son A. Martel Scott patented it in 1946, and the family still bottles it. David Cecelski's account has him catering a barbecue for President Franklin Roosevelt at the White House in 1933.

name: Adrian Miller
aliases: Adrian E. Miller|the Soul Food Scholar
what: A Denver writer and lawyer, the 'Soul Food Scholar' of his own site, whose Black Smoke: African Americans and the United States of Barbecue (UNC Press, 2021) is the history of the Black cooks, pitmasters and restaurant owners behind American barbecue and of their absence from its legends. It won the James Beard Foundation's 2022 Media Award for Reference, History, and Scholarship, his second after Soul Food (2013; award 2014). A former special assistant to President Clinton, he directs the Colorado Council of Churches and is a certified barbecue judge.

name: Bob Garner
what: A North Carolina television reporter and writer who has covered the state's barbecue since 1994, when he began short features on it for UNC-TV's magazine program North Carolina Now. His first book, North Carolina Barbecue: Flavored by Time (John F. Blair, 1996), toured the state's pits; a one-hour television special followed, and with it the name 'the barbecue man'. Bob Garner's Guide to North Carolina Barbecue (2002) and Bob Garner's Book of Barbecue (2012) came after. He writes restaurant pieces for Our State magazine and divides his time between Burlington and Raleigh.

name: Bob Melton
what: R. B. 'Bob' Melton (died 1958), a horse trader raised on a Nash County farm, cooked whole hogs for friends in an open pit on the Tar River at Rocky Mount, began selling barbecue there in 1922, and in 1924 built the shed that Wikipedia and UNC's North Carolina Miscellany call the state's first indoor, sit-down barbecue restaurant. He served finely chopped whole hog with a vinegar sauce, boiled potatoes, slaw, corn sticks, hushpuppies and Brunswick stew, and sent barbecue across the state by bus. Life magazine called him the King of Southern Barbecue in 1958, the year he died.

name: Bum Dennis
what: Latham Wade 'Bum' Dennis (June 12, 1937 – December 9, 2022) opened Bum's Restaurant in downtown Ayden in 1963 with his wife Shirley and cooked whole hogs over wood coals there for the rest of his working life, with a table of vegetables beside the barbecue that few eastern pits keep. He was of the Dennis family that counts Skilton Dennis's 1830 wagon as the start of the trade, and a kinsman of Pete Jones of the Skylight Inn. His son Larry, at the pit since he was nine, runs the restaurant.

name: Dennis Rogers
aliases: the oracle of the holy grub
what: Dennis Rogers (October 10, 1942 – August 8, 2020), a News & Observer columnist for more than thirty years, raised in Wilson and an Army veteran, who wrote about small-town eastern North Carolina and its soldiers and, in barbecue, spoke for the east: whole hog with vinegar and pepper and nothing else. He called himself the 'oracle of the holy grub' in a long mock war of columns with Jerry Bledsoe of Greensboro over ketchup in the sauce. His columns were collected in Home Grown (1979), Second Harvest (1981), Crossroads (1984) and It's Bad News When the Bartender Cries (1988).

name: Ed Mitchell
