what: Ed Mitchell (born 1948 or 1949) is a whole-hog pitmaster from Wilson who began cooking pigs behind his family's grocery store in the early 1990s, turned the store into Mitchell's Ribs, Chicken & Bar-B-Q, co-founded The Pit in Raleigh in 2007, and has argued for pasture-raised heritage hogs since the 2000s. The Southern Foodways Alliance recorded him in 2007; the American Royal put him in its Barbecue Hall of Fame in 2022. His book, Ed Mitchell's Barbeque, written with his son Ryan Mitchell and Zella Palmer, came out from Ecco in 2023.

name: Elliott Moss
what: Elliott Moss is a chef and whole-hog pitmaster from Florence, in the Pee Dee of South Carolina, who grew up watching his grandfather smoke hogs, moved to Asheville in 2007 to open The Admiral, and in August 2015 opened Buxton Hall Barbecue there with Meherwan Irani's Chai Pani group, bringing wood-cooked whole hog and South Carolina hash to the mountains. He left Buxton Hall in July 2022; it closed in November 2023. In 2025 he and his wife Jennifer opened Elliott's Barbecue Lounge inside Seminar Brewing in Florence, which Southern Living named the South's best new barbecue restaurant for 2026.

name: Jerry Bledsoe
aliases: Jerry Carroll Bledsoe|the world's leading, foremost barbecue authority
what: Jerry Carroll Bledsoe (July 14, 1941 – December 31, 2025), a Greensboro newspaper columnist and author, born in Danville, Virginia and raised in Thomasville, who wrote for the Greensboro Daily News, later the News & Record, for twenty-three years and became a true-crime writer with Bitter Blood (1988), a number-one New York Times bestseller. In barbecue he was Lexington's man: the self-styled 'world's leading, foremost barbecue authority' in a decades-long mock war of columns with Dennis Rogers of the Raleigh News & Observer over ketchup in the sauce.

name: Jess Swicegood
what: Jess Swicegood ran a barbecue stand a few yards from Sid Weaver's tent by the Lexington courthouse in the 1920s, taught Warner Stamey pit cooking alongside Weaver, and sold Stamey the business in 1938 — for $300, by Robert Moss's account — when Stamey came back from Shelby and renamed it Stamey's. Through that sale the Swicegood stand is the ancestor of Stamey's in Greensboro and, through Stamey's pupil Wayne Monk, of Lexington Barbecue. He is spelled Jess and Jesse in the sources, and no dates of birth or death are on record here.

name: Jim Early
what: James Howard Early Jr. (1939–2021), a Winston-Salem lawyer and cook who founded the North Carolina Barbecue Society in 2006 and led it until his death. His self-published guide, The Best Tar Heel Barbecue: Manteo to Murphy (2002), came out of a search through all hundred counties for pits still cooking pork over wood coals; the society's Historic Barbecue Trail is that list under rules he wrote — wood or charcoal on grates, a house sauce, fifteen years' cooking, no more than two stops in a town.

name: Joe Bessinger
aliases: Joseph Jacob Bessinger|Big Joe Bessinger|Joseph Bessinger Sr.
what: Joseph Jacob 'Big Joe' Bessinger, a farmer from Orangeburg County, traded the family cow, a mule and fifty dollars for a cafe in Holly Hill and opened it in 1939 serving pork with a mustard-based sauce — the Golden Secret, his family calls it, worked out with the Sweatman family on shared German roots. Five of his sons opened barbecue restaurants on it: Maurice and Joe Jr. at West Columbia in 1953, Melvin and Thomas in Charleston from 1955, and, by two accounts, Robert. Some name him the inventor of South Carolina's mustard sauce; the evidence names no one.

name: John Shelton Reed
what: A sociologist of the American South, born 1942, who taught at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill from 1969 until 2000 and retired as William Rand Kenan Jr. Professor. With his wife Dale Volberg Reed and William McKinney he wrote Holy Smoke: The Big Book of North Carolina Barbecue (UNC Press, 2008); alone, Barbecue: A Savor the South Cookbook (2016) and On Barbecue (2021). In 2013 he and Dan Levine founded the Campaign for Real Barbecue, which certifies restaurants that cook their local style over wood alone. He lives in Chapel Hill.

name: Lake High
aliases: Lake E. High Jr.|Lake Edward High Jr.
what: Lake E. High Jr. of Columbia, a wine judge and, in his own account, a born critic, who founded the South Carolina Barbeque Association with the psychologist Walter Rolandi in 2004 to train judges and promote the state's barbecue, and wrote its history: A History of South Carolina Barbeque (The History Press, 2013). His account gives South Carolina all four of the barbecue sauces he counts — vinegar-and-pepper, mustard, light tomato and heavy tomato — each with a region and a date, and the association publishes them as a map.

name: Maurice Bessinger
aliases: Lloyd Maurice Bessinger Sr.|L. Maurice Bessinger
what: Lloyd Maurice Bessinger Sr. (July 14, 1930 – February 22, 2014) opened Maurice's Piggie Park, a drive-in, in West Columbia in 1953 with his brother Joe Jr., built it into a chain, and bottled his father's mustard sauce as Carolina Gold for supermarkets nationwide. He refused Black customers until the suit that became Newman v. Piggie Park Enterprises (1968), ran for the legislature in 1964 and for governor in 1974, and raised the Confederate flag over his restaurants on July 1, 2000, the day it came off the State House dome. His children took the last flags down in 2013.

name: Pete Jones
what: Walter B. 'Pete' Jones (died 2006) opened the Skylight Inn in Ayden, Pitt County, in the summer of 1947 — at seventeen by his family's count, eighteen by Wikipedia's — and cooked whole hogs over wood coals there for nearly sixty years. He learned the trade at his uncle Emmitt Dennis's City Cafe, counted his barbecue back to a Dennis ancestor's wagon, and put a copy of the U.S. Capitol dome on his roof after National Geographic called the place the barbecue capital of the world. The James Beard Foundation made the restaurant an America's Classic in 2003.

name: Rien Fertel
what: A New Orleans writer and historian — a Tulane doctorate in history, 2013 — who recorded the Southern Foodways Alliance's barbecue oral histories in North Carolina in 2011 and South Carolina in 2012, then spent five years following the whole-hog pitmasters of Tennessee and the Carolinas for The One True Barbecue (Touchstone, 2016): part travelogue, part memoir, about the cooks who fire, flip and chop 200-pound pigs in smoke-filled pit houses, from Rodney Scott of Hemingway and Sam Jones of Ayden to Ricky Parker of Lexington, Tennessee.

name: Robert F. Moss
what: A food writer and historian in Charleston — a Furman graduate with a doctorate in English from the University of South Carolina — who is contributing barbecue editor for Southern Living and was restaurant critic for the Post and Courier. Barbecue: The History of an American Institution (University of Alabama Press, 2010; revised and expanded 2020) is a documentary history of the subject built from newspapers, letters, diaries and travel narratives; Barbecue Lover's the Carolinas (2015) is his guide to both states. He counts South Carolina's sauces as two, mustard and vinegar, where the state's association counts four.

name: Rodney Scott
what: Rodney Scott (born November 1, 1971) is a whole-hog pitmaster from Hemingway, in the Pee Dee of South Carolina, who cooked his first pig at eleven at his parents' store, took the business over in 2011, and in February 2017 opened Rodney Scott's Whole Hog BBQ in Charleston with Nick Pihakis. In 2018 the James Beard Foundation named him Best Chef: Southeast, the second pitmaster to win a Beard chef award. His book with Lolis Eric Elie, Rodney Scott's World of BBQ, came out in 2021. Every Rodney Scott's location closed in May 2026; he cooks pop-ups as Pitmaster Scott.

name: Sam Jones
what: Samuel 'Sam' Jones is the grandson of Pete Jones and a third-generation pitmaster of the Skylight Inn in Ayden, where he sold chopped pork as a child. With Michael Letchworth he opened Sam Jones BBQ in Winterville on November 10, 2015, and a second restaurant in Raleigh in February 2021. His book with Daniel Vaughn, Whole Hog BBQ: The Gospel of Carolina Barbecue (2019), writes the family method down. He was a James Beard semifinalist for Best Chef: Southeast in 2018, and Sam Jones BBQ holds a Michelin Bib Gourmand from the first Michelin Guide American South (2025).

name: Sid Weaver
what: Sid Weaver sold barbecue from a tent across from the Davidson County courthouse in Lexington from 1919 — cooked in the alley behind, sold to people on their way to court — and is the first name in every account of Lexington-style barbecue. Jess Swicegood set up beside him within the decade; the two taught Warner Stamey, and Weaver's hand Alton Beck built the town's first permanent barbecue restaurant in 1938. What is known of him is the tent, the date, the pupils and the sauce that came out of those stands: vinegar and pepper with ketchup, the Piedmont's dip.

name: Skilton Dennis
what: Skilton Dennis is the ancestor the Dennis and Jones families of Ayden name as the start of barbecue for sale in North Carolina: by their account he sold smoked hog meat and cornbread from a wagon in 1830, and Otter Dennis, of the same family, founded the town. The 1830 is painted on the Skylight Inn's billboard as one of its four tenets and was recorded from Bum and Larry Dennis by the Southern Foodways Alliance; Bob Garner's 2012 profile of Pete Jones puts the covered wagon in the mid-1800s. No document has been produced.

name: Warner Stamey
what: Charles Warner Stamey (born 1911), the youngest of eleven children, learned pit-cooking as a high-school boarder in Lexington from Jess Swicegood and Sid Weaver at their tents across from the courthouse, sold barbecue in Shelby through the 1930s, came back in 1938 to buy Swicegood's stand and rename it Stamey's, and in 1953 opened the Greensboro drive-in his family runs. His restaurant credits him with putting hushpuppies beside barbecue in North Carolina. Wayne Monk, Red Bridges and his brother-in-law Alston Bridges learned under him; the American Royal made him a legacy inductee of its Barbecue Hall of Fame in 2020.

name: Wayne Monk
what: Wayne Monk opened Lexington Barbecue beside U.S. 29/70 in Lexington, Davidson County, in 1962, at twenty-six, after years as a carhop and then a pit hand under Warner Stamey, and he owns it with his son Rick. The pit cooks pork shoulders over oak and hickory coals and serves them with the dip, the Piedmont's thin red vinegar sauce; locals call it the Honeymonk, from his name and his early partner Sonny Hunneycutt's. He cooked for the heads of government at the 1983 economic summit in Williamsburg, and the James Beard Foundation named the restaurant an America's Classic in 2003.

name: Wilber Shirley
what: Wilberdean 'Wilber' Shirley (1930–2021) learned barbecue at Griffin's in Goldsboro, bought the former Hill's Barbecue on U.S. 70 east of town in 1962 and put his name on it, and cooked split whole hogs over oak coals there for more than forty years. Wilber's fed presidents, governors and senators and, on a holiday weekend, up to 130 pigs. It closed in March 2019 over unpaid taxes; a group of customers bought it and reopened it in July 2020, while he lived. He died on April 5, 2021, at ninety.

name: Campaign for Real Barbecue
what: A campaign, founded in 2013 by the sociologist and barbecue writer John Shelton Reed and the blogger Dan Levine, that certifies restaurants which cook the barbecue style traditional to their area and rely solely on wood for heat, and gives them a certificate and a decal. It began in North Carolina — about seventy places certified by January 2018 — and has regional 'smoke detectors' for South Carolina, Kentucky, Georgia, Alabama and the Virginia–Washington region under a True 'Cue USA program. Its three stated goals are to celebrate wood-cooking, to honor the places that keep it, and to teach eaters the difference between wood-cooked barbecue and what it calls 'faux 'cue'.

name: North Carolina Barbecue Society
what: A non-profit founded in 2006 in Winston-Salem by Jim Early, a lawyer and cook, to promote North Carolina's barbecue culture and, in its own words, to secure the state's place as the Barbecue Capital of the World. Its lasting work is the Historic Barbecue Trail: a route of about two dozen restaurants, some 700 miles end to end, admitted only if the meat cooks on grates over pits with wood or charcoal, the owners make their own sauce, the pits have run fifteen consecutive years, and no town has more than two. Early wrote the guidebook, The Best Tar Heel Barbecue: Manteo to Murphy, and the society ran two-day cooking boot camps three times a year.

name: South Carolina Barbeque Association
aliases: SCBA|SC Barbeque Association|South Carolina Barbecue Association
what: A judging body and booster founded in 2004 by Lake E. High Jr., a wine judge, and Walter Rolandi, a psychologist, 'to train the best BBQ judges in the world and to preserve and promote the unique nature of South Carolina Barbecue'. It runs judging seminars in Columbia that turn eaters into certified judges — more than 800 by 2015 — sanctions cook-offs across the state, eight of them listed between September 12 and October 24, 2026, and keeps a points championship for the teams. Its account of the state's barbecue is Lake High's: South Carolina as the home of all four sauces — mustard, vinegar-pepper, light tomato and heavy tomato — mapped by region.

name: Southern Foodways Alliance
what: An institute of the Center for the Study of Southern Culture at the University of Mississippi, founded in 1999 and directed since then by John T. Edge, that documents the food of the South: oral histories, films, writing, awards and events, funded by about 800 members. For the Carolinas its work is the Southern BBQ Trail, an oral-history project begun in February 2011 across nine states, whose North Carolina set includes the Skylight Inn, Parker's, Grady's, B's, Bum's, Stamey's, Short Sugar's, Red Bridges, Cook's, Clyde Cooper's, the Barbecue Center and Ed Mitchell, and whose South Carolina set holds eight interviews: Sweatman's, Scott's, Midway, Jackie Hite's, Dukes, Cooper's Country Store, Brown's and Melvin's. Each interview is a transcript with audio, free online.

name: South Carolina Festival of Discovery
aliases: Festival of Discovery|SC Festival of Discovery|Greenwood BBQ and Blues Festival of Discovery
facets: {"state": "SC", "when": "July, second weekend, Thursday to Saturday; July 9–11, 2026", "founded": "2000", "status": "open"}
what: A three-day barbecue-and-blues festival in Uptown Greenwood each July — Thursday to Saturday of the second weekend; July 9 to 11 in 2026 — hosted by the Uptown Greenwood Development Corporation. Its cook-off is sanctioned by the Kansas City Barbeque Society, the national competition body, and is billed as a South Carolina state championship with a Black Kettle hash competition beside it; the barbecue vendors fill the Main Street parking lot between Court and Seaboard avenues, and the Blues Cruise puts bands in restaurants and venues around the uptown into the night. The organizers billed 2026 as the twenty-fifth anniversary; press accounts date the first festival to 2000.

name: fundraiser barbecue
aliases: plate sale|barbecue plate sale|church barbecue|fire department barbecue|hash sale|BBQ fundraiser
what: The plate sale: a church, a volunteer fire department, a Ruritan club or a scout troop cooks pork — a whole hog or a stack of butts — and sells it by the plate on a Saturday to pay for a roof, a truck or a mission. In eastern North Carolina the plate is barbecue or barbecue chicken with slaw and bread; Back Swamp Volunteer Fire Department in Richlands sold pork or chicken plates for $10 on April 18, 2026, from 11 a.m. until the food ran out. In South Carolina the same money is often raised on hash: the Highway 34 Volunteer Fire Department outside Ninety Six cooks it in cast-iron pots and sells it by the quart to neighbors who read the notice in the paper and phone in an order.

name: Hillsborough Hog Day
aliases: Hog Day|Hog Day Festival|Hillsborough Hog Day Festival
what: A two-day barbecue festival and cook-off at River Park in downtown Hillsborough, Orange County, held since 1983 — the oldest continuing barbecue festival in North Carolina, by the Daily Tar Heel's account — and run since 2014 by the Orange County Optimist Club as a fundraiser for children's programs. A Friday evening opens it; Saturday brings the cook-off, live music, a car show, a fun run and the Pigs on Parade. In 2019 the count was 27 cooking teams, more than 100 vendors and a collective three tons of barbecue; the 2025 festival, September 13 and 14, came two months after Tropical Storm Chantal flooded the Eno riverfront and lost its 5K to the water.

name: Lexington Barbecue Festival
what: A one-day street festival on Main Street in uptown Lexington, Davidson County, each October since 1984, built on the town's pork-shoulder barbecue: up to twenty area restaurants cook and sell, several blocks close to traffic, and hundreds of other vendors sell crafts and fudge around them. Wikipedia's article says it draws as many as 200,000 people; the first festival drew 30,000 and 3,000 pounds of barbecue, and by 1994 the count was over 100,000 and 11,000 pounds. Since 2007 it holds a title from the General Assembly — Official Food Festival of the Piedmont Triad Region of the State of North Carolina. The 2026 festival is planned for October 24.

name: Mallard Creek Barbecue
aliases: Mallard Creek Presbyterian Church Barbecue|the Mallard Creek BBQ|the granddaddy of barbecues
what: The one-day church barbecue of Mallard Creek Presbyterian Church in northeast Charlotte, held on the fourth Thursday of October from 1929 to 2024 and retired in 2025 after ninety-three editions. It sold hickory-smoked chopped pork, Brunswick stew and the church's own slaw by the plate, sandwich, pound and quart — dine-in, drive-through and carry-out; a plate was $15 and a sandwich $7 in 2024 — and it was one of North Carolina's best-known political stops: a rope line in the parking field where candidates for every office from vice-president to dog catcher worked the crowd in the last weeks before an election.

name: pig pickin'
aliases: pig picking|pig pickin|pig pull|rolling a pig|hog roast
what: A party at which a whole hog is cooked for the crowd and the crowd eats it off the pig — picked by hand from the split carcass, or chopped on a block beside it. A barrow, a castrated male, or a gilt of about 80 to 120 pounds dressed weight is split and laid on a large charcoal or propane cooker for four to eight hours, under the direction of the host and whoever is helping; the meat is basted or dressed in the local sauce and served with slaw, hush puppies, baked beans, Brunswick stew or, in South Carolina, hash and rice. It is the eastern Carolinas' form of the wedding, the homecoming, the tailgate, the political rally and the fire-department fundraiser.
root: pig + pickin' (picking): the guests pick the meat off the cooked hog with their hands, and the gathering takes its name from the act

name: political barbecue
aliases: stump meeting|campaign barbecue|rally barbecue|the candidate's pig
facets: {"state": "both", "when": "election years; the weeks before a vote", "status": "open"}
what: The free feed a candidate or a party puts on to draw a crowd: a whole hog, or these days a pile of pork butts, cooked for whoever comes, with speeches or a rope line attached. It is as old as the republic in the Carolinas — the communal whole-hog barbecue fed political rallies in the colonial Carolinas and Virginia — and it has two living forms. In South Carolina the Galivants Ferry Stump Meeting in Horry County has gathered Democratic candidates on the Holliday family's land every second spring since 1880, descended from Wade Hampton's 1876 appearance there. In North Carolina the Mallard Creek church barbecue in Charlotte was the candidates' October stop from 1929 to 2024.

name: barbecue
what: The cooked meat itself — in the Carolinas, pork cooked slowly over coals or in a cooker and then chopped, pulled or sliced — and, by extension, the place that sells it and the gathering that eats it. Elsewhere in the country the same word means a grill, or a cookout of any meat; here the narrower sense is the ordinary one.
root: Taíno (Arawakan) barbacoa, a framework of sticks set on posts → Spanish barbacoa (1526, Oviedo) → English barbecue (1660s: the frame and the method; the cooked animal and the gathering by the 1700s)

name: Carolina Gold
aliases: Carolina Gold rice|Carolina Gold sauce|Carolina Gold BBQ sauce
what: Two South Carolina things with one name. The sauce: the yellow-mustard barbecue sauce of the Midlands — mustard, vinegar, sugar and spices — which Wikipedia says is sometimes called Carolina Gold and which Maurice Bessinger of Piggie Park sold in supermarkets under that brand. The rice: an heirloom variety of Oryza sativa named for the gold of its unhulled grain, grown in the Lowcountry by enslaved people from the 1780s, the staple of Lowcountry cooking, last harvested commercially in 1927 and revived from a seed bank in the 1980s.
root: Carolina + gold. For the rice, the colour of the unhulled grain (Wikipedia); for the sauce, the colour of yellow mustard and the brand name under which Maurice Bessinger's Piggie Park sold it (Wikipedia). Two coinages, one name, no common root but the state

name: chopped
what: The way most Carolina barbecue reaches the tray: cooked meat cut across on a block with cleavers — in the east fine enough to hold the thin vinegar sauce, in the Piedmont in larger pieces. At a Lexington counter it is an ordering word with a scale, chopped, coarse chopped, sliced, and each is a different plate from the same shoulder. 'Sliced' is the far end, the shoulder cut into slabs and not chopped at all. A whole hog is chopped all together, skin included, so that every tray gets every part.
root: chop (v.), mid-14c., 'to cut with a quick blow', of uncertain origin, perhaps Old North French choper or Old French couper 'to cut'; the noun 'a slice of mutton, lamb or pork' from the 1630s. Coarse chopped: the same, in larger pieces. Minced: Old French mincier 'to chop in little pieces', in English cooking from the late 14c. Sliced: the far pole — not chopped at all

name: dip
what: The Lexington word for its sauce: vinegar, water, ketchup or tomato, salt, black and red pepper, sugar to taste — thin enough to pour, reddish rather than red. It goes on the chopped shoulder at the counter, sits on the table in a bottle, and is the dressing of the red slaw. Each pit's recipe is its own and, the town's own article says, closely guarded; the taste runs from tangy to slightly sweet or spicy. The eastern sauce is the same idea without the tomato, and is not called dip.
root: dip (v.), Old English dyppan 'to plunge, immerse', from Proto-Germanic *daupejanan, a causative of *deup- 'deep'; the noun 'act of dipping' 1590s, 'liquid into which something is to be dipped' 1825; also in the 19th century 'a sweet sauce for pudding' and 'the juices and fat left after cooking meat'; the party dip of 1962 is, etymonline says, probably a re-coinage

name: Down East
what: In North Carolina, the coastal plain east of Raleigh — the barbecue east, where the hog is cooked whole and the sauce has no tomato; eastern North Carolina barbecue is also called Down East barbecue. The narrow sense is the string of fishing communities east of Beaufort in Carteret County — Bettie, Otway, Straits, Harkers Island, Gloucester, Marshallberg, out to Cedar Island — and Wikipedia says the phrase has broadened to mean eastern North Carolina generally, the central coastal plain of Greenville, Goldsboro, Kinston, New Bern, Rocky Mount, Tarboro, Washington and Wilson.
root: down + east, a sailing direction. Along the New England coast the summer wind is south-westerly, so a ship bound east from Boston runs downwind, and Maine was Down East (Wiktionary; Wikipedia). In North Carolina the same phrase names the coastal communities east of Beaufort in Carteret County and, broadened, the eastern part of the state (Wikipedia)

name: Dutch Fork
what: The land between the Saluda and the Broad rivers above their meeting at Columbia, in Lexington, Newberry and Richland counties, settled by German-speaking Protestants in the middle of the eighteenth century and named for them, Dutch for deutsch. It is the upstream end of the mustard belt: the yellow mustard barbecue sauce of the Midlands is linked to the German families who settled between Orangeburg County and Newberry County, and the Fork is the Newberry end of that line. Lutheran churches, place names and family names are what remains of the German; the dialect is gone.
root: Dutch, in its older English sense 'German': from the late 14th century Dutch meant German and the non-Scandinavian continental Germanic peoples generally, from Middle Dutch duutsch, cognate with German deutsch, from Proto-Germanic *theudo 'of the people'; the sense narrowed to the Netherlands around 1600 in England, but in America the older sense lasted, as in Pennsylvania Dutch (etymonline) + fork, Old English forca from Latin furca, of rivers from 1753 (etymonline): the land between the Saluda and the Broad, which join to form the Congaree at Columbia

name: fixins
what: The sides and trimmings that come with the meat: slaw, hushpuppies or cornbread, boiled potatoes in the east, hash and rice in South Carolina, pickles, sweet tea. 'Fixings' is American English of 1839 for the garnishing of a meal; fixins is how it is said and, on Carolina signs and menus, how it is spelled. Beth Tartan wrote of a Raleigh hostess telephoning Melton's — 'Ride me a party' — and Melton's putting barbecue and fixings on the bus to her.
root: fix (v.), late 14c., from Old French fixer, Latin fixus 'fastened' → fixing, verbal noun, 'act of putting in order', c. 1600 → fixings, American English, 'apparatus' 1820, 'food, garnishing' 1839 (etymonline); spelled fixin's or fixins for the g that Southern speech drops

name: hog
what: In Carolina barbecue speech the animal is a hog. Whole hog is the eastern North Carolina and Pee Dee style; a hog killing is the winter work of the farm; a hog's size is its dressed weight. American dictionaries make a hog a domesticated swine of 120 pounds or more raised for market and a pig the younger, smaller animal; the pit's small hogs of 80 to 120 pounds dressed sit at the bottom of that range. The pig pickin' hog is a barrow, a castrated male, or a gilt, a young female — boars and sows are too big.
root: Old English hogg, implied in the late-12th-century hogaster and written hogge by the mid-14th century; origin uncertain — a Celtic source (Welsh hwch, Cornish hogh 'swine') is proposed, and the OED, quoted by etymonline, calls it improbable. The original sense was age, not species: a castrated male, or a swine reared for slaughter at about a year old; stockmen also said it of yearling sheep and horses

name: light bread
what: The Southern name for white yeast bread — a store loaf or a soft bun — as against cornbread, biscuits and pone, a dense cornmeal cake. On a Carolina barbecue tray it is what the sandwich is built on: chopped barbecue and slaw on a soft white bun. At the Skylight Inn the sandwich is on a white roll; Dukes buffets in South Carolina set out white bread beside the hash. Dictionary.com labels the term Midland and Southern U.S., and defines it as white bread or any bread leavened with yeast.
root: light (adj.), Old English leoht 'not heavy', from Proto-Germanic *lingkhtaz — of bread, risen with yeast, against the dense pone and quick breads of cornmeal — + bread. Midland and Southern American English for white bread, or any bread leavened with yeast (dictionary.com); 'Southern US: white bread' (Wiktionary)

name: Pee Dee
what: The river and the region. The Pee Dee rises in the North Carolina mountains as the Yadkin, takes the name Pee Dee below the mouth of the Uwharrie, crosses into South Carolina and reaches the sea at Winyah Bay. The region is the state's north-east corner — Chesterfield, Darlington, Dillon, Florence, Marlboro and Marion counties always, Horry, Georgetown and Williamsburg usually. Its barbecue is whole hog over hardwood coals, sometimes skinned first with the skin fried, and a sauce of vinegar, salt and pepper that Wikipedia calls virtually identical to eastern North Carolina's.
root: from the Pee Dee (Pedee) people, an Indigenous nation of the South Carolina Piedmont and the river valley; the river took their name and the region took the river's. Their language was never recorded and the name's meaning is unknown

name: Piedmont
what: The plateau between the coastal plain and the Blue Ridge, from New York to Alabama and nearly 300 miles wide in North Carolina; its eastern edge is the fall line, where rivers drop off hard rock onto the soft plain and towns grew at the head of navigation. In North Carolina barbecue, Piedmont style is Lexington style — pork shoulder, a red vinegar-and-ketchup dip, red slaw — and 'Western' means the same. In South Carolina the Piedmont is the Upstate, Greenville, Spartanburg and Anderson, where the sauce is a thin ketchup and vinegar and the hash is pork and beef.
root: Italian Piemonte, from medieval Latin Pedemontium, ad pedem montium, 'at the foot of the mountains' — Latin pes, pedis 'foot' + mons, montis 'mountain' — the region below the Alps, in documents from the end of the twelfth century (Wikipedia); through French Piémont; applied to the American plateau at the foot of the Appalachians as piemont in 1755, with the d by 1855, and extended to the foot of other ranges by 1860 (etymonline)

name: pit
what: The place the cooking happens. First a trench in the ground filled with hardwood coals, the split hog on a rack above; then a wide, shallow container of cinder block, brick or steel above ground, still a pit; then, at many places, a gas cooker, still the pit. The word also names the room, the building — a pit house — and the restaurant, as in Backyard BBQ Pit or Dickey's Barbecue Pit. A smokehouse is a different building: a windowless outbuilding where hams and bacon are cured in cold smoke for weeks, not a place a meal is cooked.
root: Old English pytt 'a hole in the ground, water hole, well, grave', a Germanic borrowing of Latin puteus 'well, pit, shaft'; the barbecue sense keeps the hole's name after the hole has become a box of brick or cinder block above ground, and then a gas cooker inside a building

name: pitmaster
what: The person who runs the pit — the fire, the coals, the turning of the hog, the call that it is done. A recent word for an old job. Wiktionary defines it as one who operates a barbecue pit and adds that it is used as a term of respect; dictionary.com dates it 1980–85; Wikipedia titles its articles 'Ed Mitchell (pitmaster)' and 'Rodney Scott (pitmaster)', and BBQ Pitmasters has been on cable since 2009. In the Carolinas the older words are the cook and the pit man, and a place is known by a family's name before any title.
root: pit (Old English pytt, the cooking pit) + master (Old English, from Latin magister 'chief, teacher'; 'a workman qualified to carry on a trade on his own account' from c. 1300), on the pattern of quartermaster and the other -master compounds for the person in charge of a thing

name: pulled pork
what: Pork cooked slowly over coals or in a cooker until it comes off the bone in strands, then taken apart by hand or with forks rather than cut. Outside the Carolinas it is the name of the dish, and the dish is a shoulder — the Boston butt, the upper shoulder, is the cut it almost always means. Inside the Carolinas the meat is called barbecue, and 'pulled' is one answer, with 'chopped' and 'sliced', to how you want it: Memphis pulls by hand; the North Carolina east chops fine; Lexington serves it pulled or lightly chopped, leaving strands.
root: pull (v.), Old English pullian 'to pluck off (wool), to draw out', of uncertain origin + pork (n.), c. 1300, Old French porc 'pig', Latin porcus; the participle names how the cooked meat leaves the bone — pulled apart, not cut

name: slaw
aliases: cole slaw|coleslaw|cold slaw|barbecue slaw|red slaw|white slaw
what: Shredded raw cabbage, dressed and served cold, on every Carolina barbecue tray and most sandwiches. East of Raleigh the dressing is mayonnaise or whipped salad dressing and the slaw is white or yellow; in Lexington it is vinegar, ketchup and pepper — the dip — and the slaw is red, also called barbecue slaw. South Carolina buffets list coleslaw among the sides. The word is the back half of coleslaw, and the front half is not said; coleslaw came to the colonies with the Dutch settlers of New York.
root: Dutch koolsla 'cabbage salad' — kool 'cabbage' (from Latin caulis) + sla, clipped from salade (from French) — → American English cole slaw, 1794, heard and written as 'cold slaw' → slaw, the back half alone, by the 1860s

name: barbecue postcards
what: Between about 1930 and 1945 an American restaurant could order its own postcards by the thousand. A printer took a photograph, had an artist colour it by hand, and ran it on paper with a woven texture — the linen card, whose surface takes bright ink and softens a plain building into something worth mailing. Roadside businesses on the highways through both Carolinas bought them and set them by the register. The caption on the back names the route number, because that is how a customer found the place again.

name: the pig that serves itself
aliases: cannibal pig|suicide food|the self-serving pig|pig in a chef's hat
what: A barbecue sign on which the pig is not the meat but the staff: a pig in a chef's toque carrying a covered tray, a pig in an apron at a pit, a pig in sunglasses eating a pork sandwich, a pig holding the restaurant's own name over its head. The animal about to be served is drawn recommending the meal, and the joke is never explained on the sign because it does not need to be. The form runs from nineteenth-century trade cards to lit plastic on a bypass, and both Carolinas are full of it.

name: The FSA photographs of Carolina eating
aliases: Marion Post Wolcott in the Carolinas|FSA/OWI Carolina photographs|the 1939 Farm Security Administration series
what: The Farm Security Administration — a New Deal agency for rural poverty — kept photographers on the road from 1935, and their negatives went to the Library of Congress as federal work, free of copyright. Marion Post Wolcott worked North and South Carolina in 1939. What survives of Carolina eating is the occasion rather than the pit: a corn shucking at Tally Ho, near Stem in Granville County, North Carolina, with the tables that followed it; ministers and deacons at an outdoor picnic near Yanceyville; and a Fourth of July on St. Helena Island, South Carolina, shot on Kodachrome, which was new.

name: the pig mascot
aliases: the smiling pig|the house pig|Little Joe|the roof pig
what: One pig, drawn once, used everywhere a barbecue business puts its name: the sign, the menu, the sauce label, the takeout box, the trailer door, the roofline, the weather vane. It is standing, smiling and usually dressed. It has no job in the picture — it is neither cooking nor eating — and that is what separates it from the pig that serves itself. A mascot is an identity: a customer who sees a pig on a bottle in a grocery aisle is meant to think of a particular pit in a particular town.

name: Pigs in the City
what: Life-sized pig sculptures, painted by artists and set out on the sidewalks of Lexington, Davidson County. Uptown Lexington, Inc. — the non-profit set up to bring business back to the town centre — ran the first exhibition in 2003 with twenty pigs, each sponsored by a business for $1,000, which paid for the whole thing. More than 40,000 people came that first year. The pigs are fibreglass blanks, identical until the artist gets them, and they come back painted as anything: a fire engine, a bulldozer, a jigsaw puzzle, a winged horse. Retired ones stay out around town.

name: Going the whole hog — the 1830s barbecue lithographs
aliases: The Political Barbecue|Going the Whole Hog|Jackson-era barbecue cartoons
what: A small group of American political prints from the 1830s in which the barbecue is the joke and the pig is the politician. A lithograph — a print pulled from a drawing made on stone, the cheap illustrated medium of the period — could be sold loose from a shop window within days of the news. H. R. Robinson of New York issued The Political Barbecue in 1834, laying Andrew Jackson on a grid iron over a brick pit lettered PUBLIC OPINION, with one bystander remarking that in South Carolina it is called barbecue. Others draw out the campaign phrase going the whole hog. They are the oldest barbecue pictures this project can show.

name: roadside barbecue signs
what: The sign a barbecue place puts at the road: a steel pylon with a lit box on top, neon or bulbs picking out a name, a bottler's disc above it, and a changeable letterboard underneath for the day's news. Most spell the word Bar-B-Q, hyphenated, because three short units fit a tall narrow cabinet better than nine letters do. What survives in photographs that anyone may reuse comes almost entirely from one man's slides: John Margolies drove American highways from the late 1960s to 2008 photographing exactly this, and the Library of Congress bought the archive and the rights with it.

name: Where all of this came from
what: Everything on this site is built from things anyone can open: public-domain cookbooks, openly licensed encyclopaedias and photographs, open map data, oral histories published by the people who recorded them, and the directories that businesses list themselves in. This page is the list, so a reader can check the work or go further than we did.

name: How to order
aliases: what to say at the counter|ordering
what: At a Carolina barbecue counter the words are short and they mean particular things. Barbecue is the meat, not the event. A tray has no bread; a plate does. Chopped, coarse chopped and sliced are three different textures off the same shoulder. Outside brown is the crust and you have to ask for it. This is the vocabulary, west and east, with what it gets you.

name: The Great Divide
aliases: east vs west|the barbecue war|vinegar vs dip
what: North Carolina cooks barbecue two ways and has never agreed to disagree about it. East of Raleigh the whole hog goes on the pit and the sauce is vinegar, salt and pepper with no tomato in it. In the Piedmont only the shoulder goes on, the sauce gets ketchup and a little sugar, and the slaw turns red because it is dressed with that sauce. The argument between them has run in newspapers, been put to a vote in the General Assembly, and is conducted daily at lunch counters in both places.
